title: Early Signs the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism Is Reshaping EU-India Steel Trade
affiliations: University of Edinburgh - Edinburgh Business School, Singapore Management University, World Bank Group and University of Edinburgh Business School

detail.title: Early Signs the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism Is Reshaping EU-India Steel Trade
detail.abstract: This study examines early signals of the EU CBAM's impact on iron and steel exporters from India by integrating firm-level export data with third-party estimates of manufacturers' emissions and production. Changes in trade flows and pricing during the CBAM reporting phase indicate that high-emission-intensity firms have decreased both their average unit prices and shipment sizes to the EU, while low-emission-intensity firms have not changed shipment behavior and may have benefited from increasing prices. Such supply chain adjustments are in line with EU policy intentions, creating opportunities for low-emission producers while reducing reliance on high-emission suppliers to the EU.

title: Advanced Machine Learning for Robust Botnet Attack Detection in Evolving Threat Landscapes
affiliations: University of Illinois at Springfield, Fairleigh Dickinson University, University of Illinois at Springfield, University of Houston, Sacred Heart University and University of Bridgeport

detail.title: Advanced Machine Learning for Robust Botnet Attack Detection in Evolving Threat Landscapes
detail.abstract: As technology advances and security issues and cyberattacks increase, extensively Internet of Things (IoT) devices are linked to networks, and botnets have been emerging and evolving very fast, and they pose a dangerous threat. As systems become more complex, scale and, therefore, more complex, cyberattacks mounted against their vulnerabilities also increase. IoT transition is disrupted using these attacks, disrupting the IoT devices' networks and services approaches for botnet attack detection and classification using Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) have been developed within the framework of the IoT. This study provides an intrusion detection system (IDS) based on the Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (Bi-GRU) for detecting botnet attacks in IoT networks. We use the N-BaIoT dataset for this purpose. The study opted for a Bi-GRU model, which can detect contextual dependencies in the past and the future, to deal with the sequential IoT traffic data. The Bi-GRU model performance achieved exceptional results in classifying network traffic. The system's accuracy in identifying both malicious and benign traffic was 99.99%. Additionally, the accuracy of these models rapidly rises and eventually levels out at almost 100%, indicating strong model performance. The model's ability to recognise various botnet attack types even in cases of data imbalance was demonstrated by important performance metrics such as ROC-AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The results show that the proposed Bi-GRU-based IDS is a robust and improved solution for detecting IoT botnet attacks on a real-time basis. While the model performs impressively, it has some problems, including the minor misclassification in complex attack cases and dependency on a single dataset, which restricts its generalisation. Future work will focus on improving model robustness.

title: Do “Environmental” Constitutions Protect the Environment?: Evidence from Ecuador
affiliations: Texas Tech University, University of Texas at El Paso and Archbridge Institute

detail.title: Do “Environmental” Constitutions Protect the Environment?: Evidence from Ecuador
detail.abstract: Left-leaning populist regimes, such as Rafael Correa's government in Ecuador (2007-2016), often claim to protect the environment from the negative effects of free-market regimes. This study examines the environmental impact in Ecuador following the 2008 constitutional amendment, which was the first in the world to include rights of nature. We find no statistical evidence that Correa's constitutional initiative had any measurable effect on Ecuador's environmental outcomes.

title: From an Interpretive Tool to Substantive Law: The Apotheosis of Good Faith in CISG Jurisprudence
affiliations: Florida State University - College of Law

detail.title: From an Interpretive Tool to Substantive Law: The Apotheosis of Good Faith in CISG Jurisprudence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
This Article offers a narrow lens of analysis: it examines the essence of an interpretive provision in Article 7’s mention of “Good Faith” in the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (“CISG” or “Convention”) and considers how that article has become glorified, ultimately rising to the deified status of substantive law by way of oftentimes creative, interpretive incorporation techniques by various domestic courts and international arbitral tribunals. Borrowing from religious terminology, court treatment of good faith over the years has resulted in the elevation and exaltation of a universal trope to a divine honor, an apotheosis. This Article argues that this elevation to an apotheosis-like status was never the original intention of the drafters of the Convention; quintessence was never contemplated. The compromise worked out at the 1980 Vienna Conference confined good faith to the interpretation of the CISG only. Good faith did not incorporate any behavioral standards by which parties’ performances under sales contracts were to be measured. Good faith was to play only a modest and limited role. The plain meaning reference to it suggests it was of emblematic value, and its placement in a provision dealing with interpretation of the Convention is somewhat surprising and strange. This perplexity continues: one cannot find a definition or explanation of good faith in the CISG. It is a compromise provision that merely formulates good faith as an interpretive device only. But this is a far cry from what it has become and the heights it has climbed.


The uncertain status and function of good faith by the drafters of the Convention appears to be deliberate: They imposed on contracting parties no substantive duty to act in good faith. Further, the placement of good faith in the CISG’s general principles also suggests that the reference to it is directed to the courts rather than to contracting parties. This outlier treatment stands in stark contrast to other international instruments, such as the Principles of European Contract Law and the UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts, both of which explicitly impose a duty of good faith on the contracting parties. Nevertheless, in CISG cases, good faith is commonly referred to in judicial decisions but in such a way as not to make it clear what good faith means or to show why there is any need to invoke it outside of its interpretive purpose.
Thus, domestic courts, international tribunals, scholars, judges and arbitrators have, at times, conflated the CISG’s interpretive provisions with its substantive ones, as this Article demonstrates with good faith. This comingling of an interpretive provision is problematic as it creates uncertainty among parties involved in international trade. The merging of different conceptions of the provision also reflects the scholarly discourse on the topic: some CISG scholars argue that the role of good faith is limited to the interpretation of the CISG only while others view good faith in the CISG as a general principle that must govern the conduct of the contracting parties. Distinctions between what is simply interpretive guidance and what is substantive law is of crucial importance to courts and tribunals in developing sound and principled jurisprudence regarding the proper application of the CISG. This Article argues that an expansive role for good faith was never contemplated by the drafters of the Convention, and a review of subsequent case law on it has neither clarified what good faith means in practice nor shown legal practitioners why it needs to be invoked when the cases can be settled by other means. The current confusion over good faith creates contractual ambiguity and this lack of clarity does not auger well for the future of the CISG as a uniform sales law in international transactions.

title: Sovereign Debt as Soft Governance: IMF Veto Power, Dollar Safe-Asset Privilege, and the Distributional Costs of Conditionality
affiliations: Open Christian University and Open Christian University

detail.title: Sovereign Debt as Soft Governance: IMF Veto Power, Dollar Safe-Asset Privilege, and the Distributional Costs of Conditionality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on secondary data obtained from publicly available repositories and peer-reviewed publications. It does not involve the collection of new information from human participants or the use of live animals or animal tissues. All datasets were accessed in accordance with the terms of use prescribed by the original custodians, and no personally identifiable information is included. Consequently, the research falls outside the purview of institutional review board oversight and animal-care protocols. The authors affirm that the study complies with all pertinent ethical guidelines, legal requirements, and journal policies governing research integrity and the responsible use of data.
declarations.funderStatement: This manuscript was prepared entirely through the authors’ own efforts and resources; no external funding was received

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study proposes an integrated political-economy framework that links the global safe-asset regime centred on United States Treasury securities, the International Monetary Fund's quota-weighted veto structure, and the distributive effects of policy conditionality. It asks how these three mechanisms jointly shift adjustment costs toward low-and middle-income countries while preserving reserve-currency privilege for core creditors. Design / Methodology / Approach: A secondary, multi-method design combines (i) a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review, (ii) cross-case synthesis of Ghana and Sri Lanka, and (iii) panel System-GMM tests for 120 countries (2000-2025) augmented by synthetic-control estimates around IMF programme onsets. Findings: Results confirm three propositions: the U.S. convenience yield is large and persistent; the IMF's 85 percent super-majority rule confers de facto veto power on a small creditor bloc; and higher structural-conditionality intensity correlates with rising Gini coefficients and poverty headcount within five years of programme entry. Research Implications: The fused model offers testable pathways-from global demand for safe assets through institutional agenda control to country-level inequality-that future scholars can probe with micro-data or natural-experiment designs. Practical Implications: Policy recommendations include (i) accelerating quota and voice reform to dilute veto concentration, (ii) embedding social-spending floors and shock-contingent relief in programme design, and (iii) instituting transparent disclosure of creditor composition to facilitate equitable burden-sharing in debt workouts. Originality / Value: By unifying macro-finance, global-governance, and comparative-political-economy literatures, the article reframes "exorbitant privilege" as a form of soft governance and introduces biblical Jubilee principles-"proclaim liberty throughout the land" (Leviticus 25:10) and periodic debt release (Deuteronomy 15:1-2)-to evaluate sovereign-debt architecture, echoing the warning that "the borrower is a slave to the lender" (Proverbs 22:7).

title: Bonus or Penalty Contracts in Tournaments: A Question of Regulatory Focus
affiliations: University of Vienna - Faculty of Business, Economics, and Statistics and University of Vienna

detail.title: Bonus or Penalty Contracts in Tournaments: A Question of Regulatory Focus
detail.abstract: In this study, we examine how contract framing in the form of bonus and penalty contracts influences employee performance in tournaments. According to the regulatory focus and fit theory, people use different motivational strategies when pursuing goals. Individuals with a high dispositional promotion focus concentrate on advancement, while those with a high prevention focus concentrate on failureavoidance. In addition to these dispositional foci, a bonus (penalty) frame induces a situational promotion (prevention) focus, whereas tournaments evoke a situational prevention focus. The theory predicts that people will invest the greatest efforts to pursue a goal if there is a fit between the dispositional and situational foci. Our experimental results support this prediction. Tournament performance under a penalty contract is positively associated with an individual's prevention focus. Giving a penalty contract to individuals with a high prevention focus leads to the highest performance as they experience regulatory fit. All other combinations lead to a non-fit and to lower performance.

title: Cross Market Price Discovery and Selective Delta Hedging in the Option Market
affiliations: Queen's University

detail.title: Cross Market Price Discovery and Selective Delta Hedging in the Option Market
detail.abstract: We study the impact of option trading on equity price discovery using trade-level OPRA and TAQ data for S&P 500 stocks in 2020. On average, an option trade moves the underlying price by 0.56 basis points over five minutes, about one-sixth the effect of a stock trade. The impact is heterogeneous, increases monotonically with moneyness and absolute delta, and concentrates in single-leg and limit-order-book trades, while auction and multi-leg trades have negligible effects. These option trade characteristics associated with high price impact in the underlying are also associated with more stock limit-order-book activity within 100 milliseconds of option trades, consistent with the hypothesis where option market makers selectively delta hedge their orders.

reference: Advances in Consumer Research, Volume 2, No. 4, pp. 3567–3574 (2025).
title: Safeguarding the Digital Consumer: A Comparative Legal and Psychological Analysis of Dark Patterns in E-Commerce
affiliations: Birla Global University, Birla Global University and Student, A.K.K. New Law Academy, Pune, India

detail.title: Safeguarding the Digital Consumer: A Comparative Legal and Psychological Analysis of Dark Patterns in E-Commerce

publicationDetails.detailsText: Advances in Consumer Research, Volume 2, No. 4, pp. 3567–3574 (2025).

detail.abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce has transformed consumer markets, but alongside convenience has emerged the troubling phenomenon of "dark patterns" deceptive user interface designs that manipulate consumer decision-making. These patterns exploit cognitive biases, nudge users into unintended purchases or subscriptions, and erode consumer autonomy. This paper undertakes a comparative legal and psychological analysis of dark patterns, examining their prevalence, the vulnerabilities they exploit, and the effectiveness of regulatory responses. Drawing on legal frameworks in the United States, European Union, and India, it explores how consumer protection and data privacy laws have attempted to counter manipulative practices. Parallelly, insights from behavioural psychology demonstrate how heuristics such as scarcity bias, default bias, and loss aversion are systematically weaponized in digital marketplaces. While legal measures exist, enforcement is fragmented and often lags behind evolving technological designs. Psychological studies suggest that consumer awareness alone is insufficient, as manipulative designs operate subconsciously. The paper argues that safeguarding digital consumers requires a dual strategystrengthening legal standards and incorporating behavioural insights into regulatory design. By bridging law and psychology, this study highlights pathways for more ethical e-commerce practices and proposes measures for policymakers, businesses, and consumer advocates to curb the proliferation of dark patterns.

title: The Quest for Regulation of Uncollateralized Digital Lending in Ethiopia

detail.title: The Quest for Regulation of Uncollateralized Digital Lending in Ethiopia
detail.abstract: The availability and accessibility of credit is instrumental to startups that are in need of 'seed money' to raise investment capital. The availability of a credit system that is easy to secure is very critical. The current digital revolution has changed the traditional hurdles for accessing loan. Nowadays, technology has changed the modality and conditionality of accessing loan. Ethiopian banks and non-bank economic sectors, like Ethio-Telecom have started offering uncollateralized digital lending. The Ethio-Telecom, took the first initiative in offering easy and uncollateralized digital credit system in Ethiopia. However, the regulatory landscape is not ready to effectively to govern the increasing uncollateralized digital lending. This short article attempts to highlight the need for setting a regulatory framework that specifically suits to uncollateralized digital lending in Ethiopia by applying doctrinal research methodology.

title: Remote Work: Implications for Optimal Income Taxation

detail.title: Remote Work: Implications for Optimal Income Taxation
detail.abstract: This paper studies optimal income taxation in the context of remote work. The choice of workplace is discretely modeled, incorporating heterogeneity in workplace preferences and productivity losses associated with working from home (WFH). Optimal income taxation is examined using Ramsey taxation, both with and without WFH. The main result shows that incorporating WFH reduces the optimal marginal income tax rate. This reduction is quantitatively significant and robust across alternative specifications. In a calibrated economy, optimal marginal tax rates are about 2% to 3% lower for low-income groups and about 4% to 5% lower for high-income groups when WFH is considered in the Ramsey problem. With an additional income of $10,000, the optimal policy with WFH reduces the tax burden by $280 to $520 at income levels between $40,000 and $500,000, compared to the policy without WFH.

title: Cultural Identity and National Traditions in Ukrainian Education: Historical Perspectives
affiliations: Pylyp Orlyk International Classical University and Pylyp Orlyk International Classical University

detail.title: Cultural Identity and National Traditions in Ukrainian Education: Historical Perspectives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is theoretical in nature and does not involve human participants or personal data. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This article traces how Ukrainian cultural identity and national traditions have shaped-and been shaped by-the evolution of schooling from Kyivan Rus' to the present. We show how religious literacy and monastic learning laid early foundations; how the Cossack-Hetmanate and the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy catalysed a humanistic, Europeanfacing curriculum; how imperial Russification and Soviet ideological schooling repressed Ukrainian language and memory while provoking resilient, often clandestine, cultural transmission; and how post-1991 reforms, the Revolution of Dignity (2014), and the ongoing war have re-centred Ukrainian language, history, and civic formation. Contemporary primary curricula increasingly balance decolonising aims with competency-based, child-centred pedagogy, integrate cultural heritage across subjects, and foreground civic agency, media literacy, and socio-emotional resilience. We argue for an inquiry-driven model-co-designed with communities and inclusive of minority narratives-that treats national identity not as dogma but as living, dialogic practice.

title: Building Trust with a Teachable Artificial Intelligence: The Case of Repeated Trust Games *
affiliations: Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), Singapore University of Technology and Design and Singapore University of Technology and Design

detail.title: Building Trust with a Teachable Artificial Intelligence: The Case of Repeated Trust Games *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author(s) declare no competing interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the ethical committee of the Singapore University of Technology and Design on 3 May 2023 (IRB-23-00590)
declarations.funderStatement: The financial support received from AI Singapore Governance Grant (AISG3-GV-2021-005) is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract: This study explores the teaching of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems in a repeated trust game. We evaluate whether participants trust the AI and teach it to adopt the most beneficial strategies among a set of four options with different levels of benefit. Results indicate that participants are initially cautious with the AI but increase their trust throughout the experiment, especially those with initially low trust. Participants imperfectly teach the AI, initially adopting beneficial strategies, then progressively learning the most advantageous ones while discarding those that offer minimal or no benefit. We also observe that participants inefficiently choose to avoid positive learning when it involves a risk of large losses. In additional tasks, we observe that participants naturally seek ways to exploit the AI, although a significant portion maintains human fairness in the interaction. Moreover, they effectively transfer prior knowledge to similar tasks. We conclude that participants trust an AI they can teach to generate significant benefits, although the risk of loss limits this trust and the efficiency of teaching.

title: Property Taxes and the Great Recession: The Role of Property Tax Limits
affiliations: Tax Policy Center

detail.title: Property Taxes and the Great Recession: The Role of Property Tax Limits
detail.abstract: Using 2000-2016 county-level data from 39 states, we study how falling home prices affected property tax revenues under various property tax limits. Revenues adjusted gradually, reflecting lags in assessments and millage offsetting. With national shocks absorbed, responses to positive and negative base changes were broadly symmetric, though specifications without year effects suggest stronger offsetting in downturns. Assessment limits cut the passthrough from home prices to taxable values by nearly half, while combined assessment and rate limits pushing systems toward rate-driven taxation. States with levy limits had lower passthrough coefficients between assessed values and revenues.

title: Context Dependence in Managerial Expectations
affiliations: Yale School of Management

detail.title: Context Dependence in Managerial Expectations
detail.abstract: This paper examines the biases in managerial expectations as a function of firms' financial conditions. Using microdata from the Duke CFO Survey and managerial guidance, I document pervasive overreaction to news across forecasts of firm profitability, operations, and financing decisions, and even the aggregate market returns. Forecast errors are predictable from past realizations, consistent with extrapolative belief formation. I demonstrate that these biases are context-dependent: overreaction is stronger among financially constrained firms. Using exogenous shocks to earnings and financial conditions, I show that constrained managers overreact more strongly to negative earnings news, while managers with improved financial conditions exhibit weaker overreaction to positive earnings news. Evidence from moderate earthquakes as exogenous emotional shocks supports an affect-based mechanism: negative emotions distort managerial expectations, and these expectations, in turn, influence managers' future investment decisions. Overall, the results uncover novel affect-driven channels through which managerial expectations amplify distortions in firm investment.

title: The Effect of Human Resource Planning on Organizational Performance- A Study of Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund
affiliations: Adejugbe and Co Law Firm and Adejugbe and Co Law Firm

detail.title: The Effect of Human Resource Planning on Organizational Performance- A Study of Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund
detail.abstract:
Human resource planning (HRP) is a critical driver of organizational performance as it ensures the right number of employees with the appropriate skills are available to achieve strategic objectives. In Nigeria’s public sector, however, HRP is often undervalued, leading to challenges such as inadequate succession planning, high staff turnover, skills shortages, and declining productivity. This study examines the effect of HRP on organizational performance with specific focus on the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF).

The study is anchored on the Resource-Based View (RBV) and Human Capital Theory. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. Data were collected from employees of NSITF using stratified random sampling to ensure balanced representation across staff categories. Structured questionnaires served as the primary data collection tool, complemented by secondary sources. Reliability and validity were established through pilot testing and expert review. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and regression analysis with the aid of SPSS software.

Results show that effective HRP practices such as manpower forecasting, recruitment and selection, training and development, and succession planning—positively and significantly impact organizational performance. These practices enhance employee motivation, commitment, and productivity. Conversely, inadequate planning systems, poor communication, and weak succession structures were identified as barriers to performance.

The study concludes that HRP is indispensable for sustaining organizational growth, productivity, and competitiveness within Nigeria’s public sector.

The research recommends strengthening manpower forecasting, institutionalizing continuous training and career development, adopting robust succession planning frameworks, and ensuring effective communication and adequate funding for workforce development. These measures will enhance service delivery, improve employee retention, and promote long-term organizational effectiveness.

title: Modern Strategies for Management of Business, Economy, Services vis-a-vis Social Sciences-A Sustainable Approach Changing Role of Human Resources Management

declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable

detail.abstract: An old saying, "Time will never be the same," perfectly fits Human Resource Management (HRM). There was a time during the industrialization phase when the most important resource of a company, the human workforce, was exploited for the sake of production. Time changed, and HR spawned in the early 20th century, influenced by Frederick Taylor, gaining attention from many scholars and establishing itself as a new field. This paper explains the changing role of HRM under seven sections.

title: A Simple Characterization of Qualified Majority Voting Rules
affiliations: Budapest University of Technology and Economics

detail.title: A Simple Characterization of Qualified Majority Voting Rules
detail.abstract: This paper characterizes every qualified majority voting rule with a quota q strictly greater than half of the voter set in environments with just two alternatives through anonymity, responsiveness, and q-neutrality. Crucially, the latter imposes independence of the labels of the alternatives only for all preference profiles in which some alternative is strictly top-ranked by at least q voters. Thus, this paper generalizes May's (1952, Theorem, p. 682) characterization of the simple majority voting rule to qualified majority voting rules with a quota q strictly greater than half of the voter set. In doing so, it shows that these qualified majority voting rules are distinguished by their degree of neutrality.

title: When Oversight Overreaches: Corporate Governance as an Anti-Evolutionary Force in Technologically Turbulent Markets
affiliations: CESAR School

detail.title: When Oversight Overreaches: Corporate Governance as an Anti-Evolutionary Force in Technologically Turbulent Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper advances a deliberately provocative thesis: in technologically turbulent markets, the modal effect of boards, compliance, and auditing is to reduce the expected survival time of firms. This is not because stewardship is undesirable, but because legacy oversight architectures, designed for an era of industrial stability, systematically mis-specify risk and slow adaptation precisely when speed and strategic recomposition determine organizational survival. We argue that the contemporary strategic landscape is no longer defined by mere turbulence but by the arrival of "Red Swans": systemic, paradigm-shifting ruptures that shatter the very frameworks of prediction and explanation. In this new reality, conventional governance is not merely outdated but ontologically unfit for the challenges of a hyperconnected, AI-accelerated world.

Drawing on a synthesis of established theories, including organizational inertia (Hannan and Freeman, 1984), path dependence (Sydow et al., 2009), and the audit expectation gap (Quick, 2020), we demonstrate how the pillars of legacy governance form a self-reinforcing "iron triangle" of inertia. This system locks firms into outdated strategic paradigms through path-dependent boards that act as "museums of best practices," compliance regimes that codify inertia into rigid routines, and firm audit practices that provide a ritualized and dangerously misleading assurance. Through a forensic analysis of major global corporate collapses (Wirecard, Carillion, Steinhoff, NMC Health, and Boeing), we trace the recurring micro-mechanisms by which this oversight apparatus actively shortens corporate survival under conditions of technological acceleration.

The argument is not nihilistic. As a constructive alternative, we propose a framework for adaptive governance grounded in the theoretical foundations of paraconsistent strategy (Meira, 2024p). This approach rejects the classical management pursuit of coherence, arguing instead that the capacity to manage, rather than eliminate, strategic contradiction is the primary source of resilience and innovation.

This paraconsistent logic is operationalized through three core design principles: boards reconstituted with structural multidexterity to govern competing business models; compliance rewired to generate productive conflictension between control and innovation; and assurance reinvented as strategic metacapability through real-time analytics. Strong governance can extend survival, but only when it is context-sensitive, digitally fluent, and oriented toward navigating rupture rather than enforcing retrospective conformity. In most fast-moving contexts today, our 20th-century oversight templates too often act like sand in the gearbox.

reference: Intangible Capital, volume 21, issue 2, 2025[10.3926/ic.3154]
title: Online Grocery Shopping in Catalonia: How Non-Targeted Surveys Can Miss the Mark
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) - Applied Economics Department

detail.title: Online Grocery Shopping in Catalonia: How Non-Targeted Surveys Can Miss the Mark

publicationDetails.detailsText: Intangible Capital, volume 21, issue 2, 2025[10.3926/ic.3154]

detail.abstract:
Purpose: The goal of the present methodological note is to show that surveys which are not targeted at primary grocery shoppers risk substantially underestimating the uptake of e-grocery services. Research based on such data is also liable to mismeasure the impact of explanatory variables. 

Design/methodology/approach: Data of Tuneu, Tarrats and Arimany-Serrat's (2023) recent survey among Catalonian consumers are repurposed. Importantly, Tuneu et al.'s survey did not require respondents to be the primary grocery shopper of their household. The present study first calculates the penetration rate of e-grocery services for the sample as is (something, to be clear, the original article does not do). Based on a novel proxy, the study then filters out the non-primary shoppers and recalculates the penetration rate. Correlations between key constructs are also recomputed. 

Findings: After the proposed correction, the penetration rate of e-grocery services is 7.3-10.3 percentage points higher. As for the factors influencing adoption, correlation coefficients can be up to six times higher. 

Research limitations/implications: Albeit an improvement over extant research, the primary grocery shopper proxy remains a proxy. Also, the approach still requires some of the same assumptions found in earlier articles, namely that all households have a primary shopper, and that many non-primary shoppers will respond to the survey as individuals-rather than as a member of their household. 

Practical implications: The takeaway for researchers is that one should explicitly consider the household nature of grocery shopping. Concretely, consumer surveys should either target individuals responsible for a substantial part of the household's grocery purchases or explicitly ask respondents to answer on behalf of their household. 

Originality/value: Compared to extant research, the method used in this note requires less bold assumptions and produces more precise estimates of the bias involved. It may also provide a way to recalculate, and thus salvage, estimates proffered by earlier studies.

title: A Critical Re-framing of the AI(s) and Sustainability Regulation Debate through the Lens of Law and Technology
affiliations: CiTiP KU Leuven and KU Leuven - Centre for IT & IP Law (CiTiP)

detail.title: A Critical Re-framing of the AI(s) and Sustainability Regulation Debate through the Lens of Law and Technology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: This research has been partly funded by the KU Leuven "FlexIQ" project (C2M/24/028)

contentType.other: English translation of the chapter published in French

detail.abstract: The current policy and legal debate surrounding AI and sustainability has developed on a binary framing for which AI technologies carry significant environmental impacts and, at the same time, they are indispensable drivers of the ecological transition. This two-sided coin concept of 'sustainable AI' is in turn intertwined with the claim that more accurate and granular data are needed, both to identify and measure AI environmental impacts and to feed AI systems broadly leveraged to fight climate change and foster the ecological transition-whatever it means. EU policy and legislation have started to provide some responses to the question of how to keep the AI sector growing, while mitigating its adverse environmental impact. EU interventions are so far rooted in a risk-based approach to regulation characterized by reporting obligations and largely focused on the energy consumption component of the overall environmental imprint of AI infrastructures. Meanwhile legal scholars are formulating normative arguments on the matter, by identifying problems and advancing possible regulatory approaches, along the binary framing of the debate. We contend that the seeming inability to think beyond the current framing of the matter generates epistemic assumptions that mislead the elaboration of the questions to be posed in the first place and of the possible regulatory solutions to these questions. In that light, we explore why this framing is prevailing and how a fresher approach can be envisaged through the lens of the law and technology branch of law-also known as cyberlaw. In particular, we showcase how the representation of the relationship between law and technology-core matter of law and technology scholarship over time-fundamentally influences how a "new" technology and the questions it carries-as AI and sustainability-are framed and dealt with from a policy and legal point of view. We retrace the characters of technological determinism, exceptionalism and solutionism, as analysed and debunked in the law and technology literature, and we applied them to the current debate of AI and sustainability, illustrating how this debate is heavily impacted by the epistemic assumptions deriving from a reactive relationship between technology and law. Specifically, we forge the concept of 'regulatory solutionism' to report on the regulatory phenomenon that avoids the confrontation of hard choices by legislators through the adoption of obligations that, on paper, exhaust the matter at hand while being devoid of any substantive-and thus meaningful-content. By debunking technological determinism, exceptionalism and solutionism at play, the analytical lens of the law & technology literature enable to change the entry point to the problem from AI technology as such to the socio and economic drivers of AI development and notably its extractivist and power dimensions. This allow to detect the object of regulation-which is not monolithic but includes both profit-driven and convivial AI-and to bring to the foreground the political and leading role that law, through democratic processes and substantive hard choices, can play in engaging with the different types of AIs and the difficult questions of their environmental impacts.

title: Data-Driven Detection of Network Threats using Advanced Machine Learning Techniques for Cybersecurity
affiliations: Fairleigh Dickinson University, University of Illinois at Springfield, University of Houston, Sacred Heart University, University of Bridgeport and University of Illinois at Springfield

detail.title: Data-Driven Detection of Network Threats using Advanced Machine Learning Techniques for Cybersecurity
detail.abstract: The more sophisticated and diverse the network threats become, the lower the conventional intrusion detection systems' precision and versatility. This work provides a Data Driven Intrusion Detection System (IDS) based on Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) in combination with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to improve features and minimize dimensionality. A significant amount of preprocessing is performed on the proposed model including missing value handling, normalization and removal of outliers for quality data. The ANN model outperformed the benchmark models Random Forest and Isolation Forest, with 97.5% detection accuracy, 99.0% precision, 96.7% recall, and 95.7% F1-score on the NSL-KDD dataset. These findings also demonstrate that the ANN-based IDS can effectively identify complex and dynamic cyber threats and solve a number of real-world cybersecurity issues. In addition, the model shows strong generalization and efficient learning over validation criteria across dynamic network environments which validates the stability and practicability of the model.

title: Remuneration of Music Creators in the Streaming Economy: Findings from Germany
affiliations: , Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg and European University Viadrina Frankfurt (Oder) - European New School of Digital Studies

detail.title: Remuneration of Music Creators in the Streaming Economy: Findings from Germany

declarations.funderStatement: The study “Remuneration of Music Creators in the Streaming Economy: Findings from Germany” has been funded by the Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media

detail.abstract: In 2023, approximately 71.7 million music tracks by around 5.4 million artists were available on the German streaming market. This research report, authored by Jana Costas and Patrick Vonderau, examines the remuneration system underlying these figures. It presents an independent, scien­tifically grounded, and open-ended investigation aimed at analyzing the current remuneration of music creators as well as exploring alternative remuneration models in the German music streaming market. The research study is based on a mixed-methods approach: a meta-study of academic and non-academic literature currently available, more than 60 qualitative interviews with stakeholders from the German music indus­try, a nationwide survey of approximately 3,000 music creators, and a quantitative data analysis of the German recorded music market spanning a period of more than 20 years. A legal opinion by Philipp Hacker on transparency in remuneration supplements the study. According to the survey results, over 74% of music creators re­port being dissatisfied with their income from music streaming. The music market exhibits a pronounced polarization in remuneration: based on the data analysis of the streaming market, more than 75% of revenues are concentrated among just 0.1% of artists, while 68% of artists generated less than 1 euro in revenue in 2023. This polarization is further reflected in other figures: 38% of surveyed music creators reported an increase in their streaming income and 35% noted an increase in their overall music-related income over the past five years. In contrast, 38% experienced a decline in overall income, and 25% decreasing streaming income. However, the current streaming-dominated music market does not fundamentally perform worse compared to the former CD market: in 2023, more than twice as many music creators earned revenues above the basic tax-free allowance compared to 2002. Who thrives and who loses out from the digital transformation of the music market is linked to systemic structures. Music streaming contributes to diversity in the German market, such as through a stronger genre balance among the top revenue-generating genres and the promotion of music creators with national repertoire, particularly within the highest revenue segment. However, it also leads to limitations, for example, affecting certain genres, newcomers, and music creators with national repertoire below certain revenue thresholds. To provide greater support for current­ly disadvantaged genres and artists, targeted measures could be introduced. A majority (75%) of survey respondents favor a user-centric model. The study calculates alternative models involving minimum stream thresholds, a superstar levy, and levies on catalog tracks and re-re­leases. 76% of music creators reported to be either completely unable to understand their streaming income or find them harder to comprehend compared to other income sources. Complex contractual and licensing chains and limited access to essential remuneration data make it difficult for music creators to fully track and effectively verify their earnings. The often-proclaimed demo­cratization of the market has not led to an equivalent democratization of market power, as music creators remain largely excluded from key negotiations and deci­sions concerning the fundamental structures of the streaming market and thus from decisions that directly affect their remuneration. There is a need for policy action to provide music creators with stronger means to assert their rights and interests through enhanced transparency and appro­priate regulatory frameworks. Based on the legal opinion, the study recommends expanding § 32e of the German Copyright Act (UrhG), establishing a Central Streaming Transparency Body, and developing binding, standardized metadata requirements. Political incentives for setting minimum standards for remuneration and contracts with rights holders are discussed.
