detail.title: Big Tech in the Courtroom: An Index of Federal Antitrust Filings
detail.abstract: From 2020 to 2025, dozens of federal antitrust cases have involved large digital platforms. This litigation index summarizes federal antitrust filings, including key motions and evidentiary rulings, procedural posture, economic and legal arguments, and remedies sought. The index offers an overview of facts and law presented in ongoing high-profile Big Tech antitrust cases.

title: Ephemeral Content and Attention Span: Psychological Effects of Instagram Stories on User Engagement
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Ephemeral Content and Attention Span: Psychological Effects of Instagram Stories on User Engagement
detail.abstract: Ephemeral content has emerged as a defining feature of social media, with Instagram Stories standing out as one of the most widely adopted formats. Unlike permanent posts, Stories are designed to disappear after 24 hours, creating a sense of urgency that alters how users process and engage with information. This study examines the psychological effects of Instagram Stories on attention span and user engagement, highlighting how temporal scarcity fosters habitual checking behaviors, emotional arousal, and heightened fear of missing out (FOMO). The analysis draws from cognitive psychology and media studies to explain why short-lived content captures fragmented attention while simultaneously encouraging deeper platform immersion. Findings suggest that while Stories may enhance immediate interaction rates, they also contribute to shortened attention spans and reinforce compulsive usage patterns. The paper concludes by considering the implications for user well-being, digital marketing strategies, and the broader evolution of online communication practices.

title: Climate Shock Transmission and Risk Inference for Kredit Evaluation (C-STRIKE)
affiliations: Justus-Liebig-University Giessen and Frankfurt School - UNEP Collaborating Centre for for Climate & Sustainable Energy Finance

detail.title: Climate Shock Transmission and Risk Inference for Kredit Evaluation (C-STRIKE)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge the funding by Frankfurter Institut für Risikomanagement und Regulierung (FIRM) e.V..

detail.abstract: Sudden and irregular climate-related risks are increasingly expected to pose significant threats to the economy and the stability of the financial system. Existing risk assessment methods in the financial sector remain insufficient to capture the complexity and abrupt nature of such climate shocks. This report provides an overview of current tools and approaches used in climate risk analysis, as well as a review of the relevant academic literature. Building on these foundations, we introduce a novel modeling framework, C-Strike, designed to capture climate risks from a bottom-up perspective while enabling top-down applications in the banking sector. The concept is illustrated through three case studies: an emission price shock, a 1-in-100 year flood in Northern Europe and a heat wave throughout Europe.

title: Green Bonds and Sustainable Investing: Trends, Challenges, and Future Outlook
affiliations: Pranveer Singh Institute of Technology, M.l.M Technical College, Department of Commerce and Management,, Birla Global University, Birla Global University and Student, A.K.K. New Law Academy, Pune, India

detail.title: Green Bonds and Sustainable Investing: Trends, Challenges, and Future Outlook

publicationDetails.detailsText: Shukla, D., Bhatti, R. K., Raj, P., Nanda, S. S., & Noorani, M. S. (2025). Green bonds and sustainable investing: Trends, challenges, and future outlook. Journal of International Commercial Law and Technology, 6(1), 335–341.

detail.abstract: The green bonds have come to play a significant role in the wandering sovereign environmental and social finance since besides offering the opportunity to fund environmental and social objectives, they aim to offer vulnerable investors an opportunity to make a responsible investment. Literature on the inclinations, opportunities, and perspectives of green bonds in terms of the debate on the currently existing literature and the measurement of the trend of regulation are the focus of the environment-underconsideration paper. The results indicate that the market of green bonds has increased in the world, and that green bonds in the place of operation and offer as of sovereign, corporate and supranational safety has been gaining pace. The analysis of the financial world has found that green bonds would offer the green premium; investors ought to accept somewhat lower yield with the effect of sustainability. The premium however, is not always constant, but is subjected to the type of issuer, certification, and maturity in the market trade. One of the fixes is governance and regulation since the government can avoid greenwashing itself and support its own image with certification and industrial reviews. It also means that the green bonds have some extent of positive contribution to make in curbing of carbon releasing and financing a viable growth especially with a well-established regulatory system. Along with this development come the problems of the absence of standardization, unequal representation of the world and the absence of markets depth in the developing nations. As the findings indicate, green bonds constitute a strong offer of financial practices to maintain the green transition, though whether they will be effective in the longterm view will be conditioned by the enhanced market regulation, accessibility, and transparency access. The current research would add to the national and policy discussion attempting to offer a way of understanding financial performance, risk distribution, and developmental benefits along with the establishment of future research possibilities in an endeavor to investigate how green bonds will become an increasingly significant part of sustainable investing decision-making.

title: Are Crypto Anti-Money Laundering Policies Effective?
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance, University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance

detail.title: Are Crypto Anti-Money Laundering Policies Effective?
detail.abstract: In a rapidly changing crypto landscape, it is unclear whether anti-money laundering policies accomplish their intended goals or are inexpedient activities. We measure criminal responses to recent enforcement actions in crypto by tracing illicit flows throughout 5.16 TB of Ethereum blockchain transactions. First, the 2022 OFAC sanctions against the Tornado Cash mixer resulted in a 60% decline in monthly volume, 33 basis points in incremental obfuscation costs, twice the probability of detection, and fewer interactions with both Western and less-regulated exchanges. Hackers and related flows switched to swaps and bridges, which are more traceable. Second, OFAC sanctions against other addresses are uncommon but have resulted in over 100,000 BTC and 155,000 ETH stuck on-chain. Third, over $1.34 billion in Tether in 1,798 addresses is frozen on-chain, causing criminals to move their related account activities to more costly services. Fourth, offshore exchange flows from Tornado Cash only decline significantly after Binance and OKX reach settlements with the U.S. DOJ, indicating that multiple forms of enforcement are often necessary. Overall, our results indicate that sanctions, particularly those regarding services, have been effective in seizing funds, moving funds to more traceable and seizable places, and raising laundering costs. Nevertheless, sanctions, freezes, and bans are relatively rare as a fraction of total criminal activity, and overseas exchanges still handle substantial non-sanctioned criminal flows. Our findings indicate specific areas for improvement that can help guide recent crypto policy and legislative proposals.

title: Making the Case for New Trade Rules
affiliations: Independent, Institute for Agriculture and Trade Policy, University of British Columbia (UBC) - Institute for Resources, Environment and Sustainability (IRES), , Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, University of Sao Paulo - Faculdade de Direito, Independent, Peking University, ETH Zurich, ETH Zürich, University of Bern - Centre for Development and Environment (CDE), Independent and University of Bern - Centre for Development and Environment (CDE)

detail.title: Making the Case for New Trade Rules

declarations.funderStatement: SNF: Swiss National Foundation see https://www.cde.unibe.ch/research/projects/agreement_on_agriculture_reimagined/index_eng.html

detail.abstract:
The world urgently needs more diversified and healthier food systems, environmentally and socially sound
agricultural practices, and more equitable economic outcomes. A central lever for recognizing the importance
of food and agriculture and moving their governance onto a fairer and more sustainable path is the legal framework for international food and agricultural trade.

The current global framework is the World Trade Organization’s (WTO) Agreement on Agriculture (AoA). The
Agreement on Agriculture Re-Imagined (AoA ReI) initiative is based on the observation that the AoA is illsuited
to the realities of today’s world. The AoA ReI initiative steps back from the WTO framework to propose
a model treaty for global food and agricultural trade. The AoA ReI Model Treaty seeks to foster global sustainable
food security across the globe, consistent with international human rights law and the Sustainable
Development Goals (SDGs). The aim is to catalyse transformative thinking and open up new space to take the
steps needed for fair and sustainable food and agricultural trade.

The present background paper draws together research and scholarship that illustrate the AoA’s shortcomings,
to which the Model Treaty responds. Section II describes some of the AoA’s inherent flaws, outlining
how it prioritized trade over social, environmental, and food security objectives. It notes how the Agreement
overlooked the specific needs of different categories of developing countries, restricting their policy space to
implement food security or other public interest policies whilst enabling more affluent countries to subsidize
their agriculture sector – usually not for public interest purposes.

Sections III, IV, and V document how the AoA has proven unable to adapt to meet economic, social, and food
security needs. Global food systems have undergone profound changes since the AoA came into force. Agricultural
production has grown and shifted geographically. Over the last three decades, trade patterns have
become increasingly globalized and complex. Climate change and new trade policies in major markets are
likely to reshape the landscape anew. Market concentration has intensified since the AoA came into force and
lack of adequate regulation has empowered large agribusiness while limiting the bargaining power of farmers
and governments alike.

Section VI reminds us that the political economy of trade is now fundamentally different to that which prevailed
at the time the WTO came into being, challenging past assumptions about the objectives and regulation
of international trade and making a new global trade regime not just desirable but urgent and necessary.

title: Tax Planning Responses to the Trade War
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

detail.title: Tax Planning Responses to the Trade War
detail.abstract: Tariff increases to protect domestic markets reduce profit margins for firms that cannot pass these costs on to their customers. Taking the 2018 trade war between the U.S. and China as a setting, we find that pass-through restricted firms compensate for losses by planning taxes more aggressively and reduce effective tax rates by over 3 percentage points. However, importing firms, which face increased scrutiny, abstain from using the tax channel to compensate for losses when they risk losing government contracts. We document an economically and statistically significant unintended negative effect of tariff increases on government corporate income tax revenues.

title: Influence Of Monetary Policy Variables on Manufacturing Firms: An Empirical Analysis of Nigerian Manufacturing Firms
affiliations: University of Calabar- Department of Banking & Finance, University of Calabar, University of Uyo, Federal University Otuoke, Nigeria and University of Calabar, Calabar Nigeria

detail.title: Influence Of Monetary Policy Variables on Manufacturing Firms: An Empirical Analysis of Nigerian Manufacturing Firms
detail.abstract: This study examined monetary policy variables and their impact on the performance of selected manufacturing firms in Nigeria. The objectives were to evaluate how money supply, the monetary policy rate, interest rate, and exchange rate influence manufacturing firm performance in Nigeria, using Dangote Group as a case study. The study used the ordinary least squares (OLS) multiple regression method to test and estimate relevant equations. The results showed a positive and significant relationship between money supply and Dangote Group's performance; the monetary policy rate also had a positive and significant effect on Dangote companies, while the interest rate had a significant negative effect on their performance. The study therefore recommended that monetary authorities should improve current macroeconomic variables, such as money supply and inflation, to enhance manufacturing sector performance. Additionally, it suggested that monetary authorities should continue adjusting the monetary policy rate to promote stability and improve the performance of Nigeria's manufacturing sector.

title: The Model of Clickbait: Fact-Checking and Endogenous Information Acquisition
affiliations: Waseda University - Graduate School of Economics

detail.title: The Model of Clickbait: Fact-Checking and Endogenous Information Acquisition
detail.abstract: I study the role of fact-checking in a two-period strategic communication game between a decision maker and a media outlet. The decision maker relies on the outlet's article to take a binary action, while the outlet may exert costly effort to acquire information before publishing. The decision maker is uncertain about the outlet's motive: the outlet might be opportunistic, caring only about attracting clicks. Fact-checking probabilistically reveals the payoff-relevant state. I highlight a trade-off between the diagnostic effect and the discipline effect that arises when the probability of fact-checking successfully revealing the state increases. Consequently, introducing fact-checking or increasing its success probability may, in some parameter ranges, reduce the decision maker's welfare.

title: Assessing Microcredit in Bangladesh with Special Reference to Grameen Bank: An Analysis
affiliations: Dhaka School of Economics, Constituent Institution of the University of Dhaka and Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University

detail.title: Assessing Microcredit in Bangladesh with Special Reference to Grameen Bank: An Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No biasedness
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethically done
declarations.funderStatement: No fund received

detail.abstract: This study investigates the systemic limitations of traditional microcredit models and proposes a refined framework, termed "Microcredit 2.0," which integrates digital finance, tailored entrepreneurial training, and responsive regulation. Design/methodology/approach: A mixed-methods approach was employed over 15 months (January 2024-March 2025) to analyze the impact of microcredit on poverty alleviation, focusing on the model implemented by Grameen Bank. Findings: The study reveals that while Grameen Bank has significantly enhanced financial inclusion, particularly for women, several structural challenges persist:  High interest rates (approximately 20%) contribute to recurring debt cycles.  Over-reliance on borrowing undermines sustainable income growth.  Only 22% of borrowers achieve sustainable entrepreneurship. Practical implications: The proposed Microcredit 2.0 framework includes:  Establishing Societal Banking: Creating channels for micro-savings directed toward micro-investments.  Digital Integration: Adopting mobile banking solutions to reduce transaction costs by 30-40%.

title: An Algorithm for Indoor Lighting Layout Optimization Using Simulated Annealing
affiliations: Nanjing Foreign Language School

detail.title: An Algorithm for Indoor Lighting Layout Optimization Using Simulated Annealing
detail.abstract: Indoor lighting is a major contributor to building energy consumption, and optimizing its layout is essential for reducing energy use while maintaining visual comfort. However, most existing studies focus on improving luminaire efficiency or daylighting design, while systematic research on luminaire layout optimization remains limited. This paper proposes an optimization method for indoor lighting layout based on the Simulated Annealing (SA) algorithm, aiming to achieve an energy-efficient lighting configuration through intelligent optimization. The method comprehensively considers lighting quality and energy consumption by constructing a multi-objective function, which is then solved iteratively using SA. A case study demonstrates that this method can effectively reduce lighting energy consumption while ensuring indoor lighting quality, offering a new approach and tool for indoor lighting design.

title: Law and Algorithm-Managed Firms
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Law and Algorithm-Managed Firms
detail.abstract: Recent technological advancements have enabled the emergence of business organizations fully managed by algorithms, such as decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) or through artificial intelligence (AI), as observed in China's online food delivery sector. These organizations are collectively referred to as algorithm-managed firms (AMFs). Given machines' capabilities in data collection and analysis, human directors are increasingly being replaced by algorithms or AI in specific sectors. This article contends that algorithms can effectively take over human directors' managerial, monitoring, and mediating roles. The diminishing role of human directors raises certain concerns of stakeholder protection. Unlike human directors, algorithm directors or managers would not consider stakeholders' interests unless clearly instructed to do so. However, the algorithm supplier and the AMFs may lack the incentives to fully consider stakeholders because they do not always internalize the social costs. To address the challenges of AMFs, policymakers need to consider different regulation strategies. First, they must choose between command-and-control regulations and target-based regulations. Command-and-control regulations often do not work well because regulators lack enough information or control over complex algorithms. Instead of setting detailed technical rules, policymakers should adopt target-based regulations that let the algorithm balance various interests and regulate its own operations. Second, policymakers should decide between entity-based and algorithm-based regulations. Algorithm-based regulation is more suitable because it prevents companies from passing costs onto society. The state could consider regulating the composition of the board of directors of the algorithm supplier to ensure that they incorporate the concerns of stakeholders' interests in the development of the algorithm. Additionally, corporate law doctrines that protect creditors and other stakeholders, such as piercing the corporate veil and limiting liability for corporate torts, must be revisited and modified because their foundational assumptions no longer align with the realities of AMFs.

title: Motives for Pro-Environmental Behavior
affiliations: University of the Bundeswehr Munich, Bard College - The Levy Economics Institute and University of Göttingen

detail.title: Motives for Pro-Environmental Behavior
detail.abstract: Not all behaviors that benefit the environment are executed based on pro-environmental motives. In a survey sample drawn from individuals in a medium-sized German town (n=774), prevalence and motives for 25 different, commonly used, and potentially pro-environmental behaviors are very heterogeneous. In multivariate regression, we find that amongst the common predictors of pro-environmental behavior, green self-image and environmental concern predict an index of pro-environmentally motivated behaviors, whereas income and age predict an index of financially motivated behaviors, but not vice versa. Lack of accounting for these motives may explain why evidence on some determinants of pro-environmental behavior is rather mixed. We further provide a "bias" test showing that not accounting for motives for behavior may lead to an inflation of the coefficient size of the predictors of pro-environmental behavior by up to 300%, but size and direction of bias varies strongly amongst the 25 behaviors analyzed.

title: Nonparametric Estimation of Self-and Cross-Impact
affiliations: École Polytechnique - Chair of Econophysics and Complex System, Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics and Imperial College London - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Nonparametric Estimation of Self-and Cross-Impact
detail.abstract: We introduce an offline nonparametric estimator for concave multi-asset propagator models based on a dataset of correlated price trajectories and metaorders. Compared to parametric models, our framework avoids parameter explosion in the multi-asset case and yields confidence bounds for the estimator. We implement the estimator using both proprietary metaorder data from Capital Fund Management (CFM) and publicly available S&P order flow data, where we augment the former dataset using a metaorder proxy. In particular, we provide unbiased evidence that self-impact is concave and exhibits a shifted power-law decay, and show that the metaorder proxy stabilizes the calibration. Moreover, we find that introducing cross-impact provides a significant gain in explanatory power, with concave specifications outperforming linear ones, suggesting that the square-root law extends to cross-impact. We also measure asymmetric cross-impact between assets driven by relative liquidity differences. Finally, we demonstrate that a shape-constrained projection of the nonparametric kernel not only ensures interpretability but also slightly outperforms established parametric models in terms of predictive accuracy.

title: The Real Costs of Communications Outages due to Infrastructure Theft or Vandalism
affiliations: Western Carolina University - College of Business

detail.title: The Real Costs of Communications Outages due to Infrastructure Theft or Vandalism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: As declared on the cover page: "This study has been underwritten by a joint effort of the NCTA –The Internet & Television Association, CTIA—The Wireless Association, USTelecom—The Broadband Association, and WIA—the Wireless Infrastructure Association. The analysis, viewpoints, and opinions expressed are those of the author alone."
declarations.ethicsApproval: No patients or participants to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: As declared on the cover page: "This study has been underwritten by a joint effort of the NCTA –The Internet & Television Association, CTIA—The Wireless Association, USTelecom—The Broadband Association, and WIA—the Wireless Infrastructure Association. The analysis, viewpoints, and opinions expressed are those of the author alone."

detail.abstract: When copper theft and vandalism cause telecommunications service outages, the societal costs to critical networks far exceed the market or replacement value of stolen or damaged property. These incidents do not just cut cables, they cut people off from commerce, education, healthcare, and public safety. Between June and December of 2024, these kinds of outages cost society of up to $188 million of foregone economic gain. This paper applies textbook willingness-to-pay (WTP) analysis to quantify these hidden costs. Unlike traditional accounting methods, the paper estimates the full economic value lost to society when households and businesses are disconnected. The findings show that every outage magnifies harm far beyond directly affected customers through behavioral realities like loss aversion and systemic network effects.  In essence, while a thief might gain a few hundred dollars from a copper theft, communities lose hundreds of millions overall. The analysis developed in this paper offers decision makers and stakeholders a framework for understanding the urgency of policy, industry, and community action to better safeguard critical communications infrastructure.

title: Chapter Twenty. Stress-Testing In Banking In The EU: Critical Issues And New Prospects
affiliations: Bank of Portugal, University of Lisbon - School of Law. Jean Monnet Chair – Economic Regulation in the EU and Nova School of Law

detail.title: Chapter Twenty. Stress-Testing In Banking In The EU: Critical Issues And New Prospects
detail.abstract: Stress tests consist of a procedure that involves subjecting an object or system to a severe amount of pressure with the purpose of assessing its resilience under extreme conditions. As such, stress tests are not an exclusive of the financial industry and were, in fact, introduced much earlier in other areas of human activity such as medicine or civil engineering. The focus of this chapter is, of course financial stress-testing, most notably microprudential bank stresstesting in the EU. Within this overall context this chapter will adopt the following sequence: after the present introduction (20.1), the following section (20.2) will serve to define our object of research, present its typologies (namely the distinction between micro and macroprudential stress tests), briefly describe its early evolution, and also succinctly introduce EU legal framework for microprudential stress-testing (including some key institutional aspects of such framework, especially as developed after the institutional reforms of 2010, arising from the Larosière Report 4). The ensuing section (20.3) will address the topic of EU-wide stress tests from three perspectives, namely (i) its implementation and the methodologies used from 2009 onwards; (ii) the outcomes of such stress-testing exercises; and (iii) a comparative analysis of

title: AI in Education -A Primer for Educators

detail.title: AI in Education -A Primer for Educators
detail.abstract: As AI reshapes education, it risks constructing a "digital cage"-a modern echo of Weber's industrial "iron cage"-that prioritizes algorithmic efficiency over human connection. This paradigm promises scale and personalization but threatens to undermine the reflective, relational slowness essential for deep learning. In this educators' primer we examine these tensions and their associated blind spots, arguing that resolving them requires moving beyond opaque systems to achieve full visibility into AI's decision making. We propose the dynamic prescriptive economics (DPE) framework for navigating this new landscape, advocating not for the substitution of human educators, but for a transformation that centers ethical design and intellectual agency. We conclude by calling for educators to become "ethical AI stewards" who actively shape technology to serve the public good and foster an equitable, human-centric learning ecosystem.

title: Equalization of Performance-Based Fees
affiliations: Kedge Capital Fund Management

detail.title: Equalization of Performance-Based Fees
detail.abstract: This note discusses the complexities of calculating periodic performance-based fees (PBF) in open-ended funds. While the basic calculation-applying a fixed percentage to gross performance-appears simple, practical challenges arise from diverse fee structures, high-water marks (HWM), varying investor entry and exit points, and differing subscription periods. These factors can lead to inequitable fee allocations and discrepancies in reported performances for investors with different entry points. Academic literature often overlooks these nuances, leaving gaps in understanding for students and practitioners. This note uses detailed examples to illustrate these challenges and explores methods funds employ to ensure fair treatment of investors. It also highlights the trade-offs of each approach, emphasizing the importance of clear fund documentation.

title: Enhancing Credit Risk Prediction: A Meta-Learning Framework Integrating Baseline Models, LASSO, and ECOC for Superior Accuracy
affiliations: Texas A&M International University, Southern University and A&M College, Angelo State University, Western Washington University and Firat University

detail.title: Enhancing Credit Risk Prediction: A Meta-Learning Framework Integrating Baseline Models, LASSO, and ECOC for Superior Accuracy

keywords: Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO)

detail.abstract: Effective credit risk management is fundamental to financial decision-making, necessitating robust models for default probability prediction and financial entity classification. Traditional machine learning approaches face significant challenges when confronted with high-dimensional data, limited interpretability, rare event detection, and multi-class imbalance problems in risk assessment. This research proposes a comprehensive meta-learning framework that synthesizes multiple complementary models: supervised learning algorithms, including XGBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Decision Tree; unsupervised methods such as K-Nearest Neighbors; deep learning architectures like Multilayer Perceptron; alongside LASSO regularization for feature selection and dimensionality reduction; and Error-Correcting Output Codes as a meta-classifier for handling imbalanced multi-class problems. We implement Permutation Feature Importance analysis for each prediction class across all constituent models to enhance model transparency. Our framework aims to optimize predictive performance while providing a more holistic approach to credit risk assessment. This research contributes to the development of more accurate and reliable computational models for strategic financial decision support by addressing three fundamental challenges in credit risk modeling. The empirical validation of our approach involves an analysis of the Corporate Credit Ratings dataset with credit ratings for 2,029 publicly listed US companies. Results demonstrate that our meta-learning framework significantly enhances the accuracy of financial entity classification regarding credit rating migrations (upgrades and downgrades) and default probability estimation. Integrating diverse baseline models within a meta-learning architecture enables the production of high-precision analytics on demand, facilitating timely and well-informed investment decisions in credit risk management.

title: Analyzing The Role of Money Market Instruments in Shaping Nigeria's Economic Development
affiliations: University of Calabar- Department of Banking & Finance, University of Calabar, Federal University Otuoke, Nigeria, University of Calabar, Calabar Nigeria and University of Calabar, Calabar Nigeria

detail.title: Analyzing The Role of Money Market Instruments in Shaping Nigeria's Economic Development
detail.abstract: This empirical work was conducted to determine the extent to which the money market influences the development of the Nigerian economy, covering the period from 1986 to 2019. The impact of Treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, and banker's acceptances issued within this timeframe was evaluated in relation to economic development in Nigeria. The study relied on secondary data, which underwent preliminary testing for multicollinearity to ensure the stability of the variables and the model. Data analysis was conducted using the OLS technique. The results revealed that commercial paper, Treasury bills, and certificates of deposit significantly influenced Nigeria's economic development, while banker's acceptances had a negative but insignificant impact. It was recommended that banker's acceptances as a money market instrument should be strengthened to contribute positively to economic growth. Financial regulators should implement policies to enhance stakeholders' understanding of money market operations and to prevent malpractices.

title: From Slavery to Stagnation: Agricultural Technology and Structural Transformation in the US South
affiliations: Academia Sinica and Sungkyunkwan University

detail.title: From Slavery to Stagnation: Agricultural Technology and Structural Transformation in the US South
detail.abstract: This study examines the long-run impact of American slavery on agricultural technology adoption and structural transformation. We argue that a higher enslaved ratio entrenched discriminatory labor market institutions, suppressed Black farm wages and reduced incentives to mechanize. Using county-level data, we show that counties with a higher enslaved ratio in 1860 shifted toward crops less exposed to labor-saving change and later lagged in tractor adoption, followed by weaker manufacturing growth. Evidence from racial wage disparities and IV-based mediation analysis supports wage suppression as the key mechanism in delaying technological adoption.

title: Strategic Response to Mandated Interoperability: Privacy Spillovers in Network Markets
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Faculty of Business Administration (Munich School of Management), Duesseldorf Institute for Competition Economics (DICE), Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management and Düsseldorf Institute for Competition Economics

detail.title: Strategic Response to Mandated Interoperability: Privacy Spillovers in Network Markets
detail.abstract: We study the strategic response of an incumbent with a data-driven business model when interoperability is mandated in a market with direct network effects. We model competition between the data-driven incumbent that offers free access to its service and a privacy-preserving entrant. Users are privacy conscious but value affiliating with a larger network. We characterize market outcomes with and without interoperability, where interoperability may induce data or privacy spillovers as user data are transferred across different services. Under interoperability, the incumbent increases its data collection level, which dilutes the entrant's business model with regard to data privacy due to privacy spillovers. For sufficiently large spillovers, the incumbent may even increase its market share. Users can also be worse off under interoperability despite interacting with a larger network. Our work highlights the unintended negative consequences of the regulation. We discuss optimal policy implementation with necessary complementary measures to circumvent these negative consequences.

title: Digital Financial Inclusion, Economic Growth, and Environmental Pollution: Evidence from Latin American Countries
affiliations: La Trobe University

detail.title: Digital Financial Inclusion, Economic Growth, and Environmental Pollution: Evidence from Latin American Countries
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of digital financial inclusion (DFI) and economic growth on CO2 emissions employing data from 15 Latin American countries from 2004 to 2021. Principal components analysis was applied to various finance variables to generate the DFI index. Evidence from different econometric estimators suggests that DFI has a significant positive effect on CO2 emissions. Country-specific analysis indicated that DFI has a significant positive effect on CO2 emissions in Brazil, Costa Rica, Honduras, and Mexico while having a significant negative effect for Argentina and Peru, with no significant effect in Chile, Ecuador, and Nicaragua. In addition, the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) was validated for the Latin American region, specifically for Chile, Honduras, and Peru. Contrarily, the U-shaped relationship exists between economic growth and CO2 emissions in Argentina, Brazil, and Costa Rica. The implications of the results for DFI and economic growth policies are discussed.

title: Passive Ownership and the Relevance of Fundamental Accounting Information: Evidence from the Value Effect
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: Passive Ownership and the Relevance of Fundamental Accounting Information: Evidence from the Value Effect
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether passive ownership has diminished the relevance of fundamental accounting information. Specifically, I examine whether passive ownership weakens the return predictability of adjusted book-to-price ratios, known as the value effect. Using firm-level panel data over the past 30 years, I document a strong negative association between the value effect and passive ownership. To test whether reduced information acquisition drives the attenuation of the value effect, I exploit the Pension Protection Act (PPA) of 2006, which spurred investments in index funds through Target Date Funds (TDFs). Using TDF flows as a proxy for capital that does not actively acquire firm-specific information, I find that the value effect weakens sharply among firms with greater exposure to TDF flows. Moreover, the negative relation between the value effect and passive ownership emerges with the passage of the PPA, with no such patterns observed in the pre-PPA period. Further supporting the information mechanism, the value effect declines more strongly when information acquisition activity is low. Collectively, the findings suggest that passive ownership has eroded the relevance of accounting information in capital markets by reducing firm-specific information acquisition.

title: Liability of Financial Supervisors (Portugal)
affiliations: Nova School of Law and University of Lisbon - School of Law. Jean Monnet Chair – Economic Regulation in the EU

detail.title: Liability of Financial Supervisors (Portugal)
detail.abstract: Tortious liability of financial supervisors (including those that exercise resolution functions) in Portugal is governed by the specific tort law regime applicable to the State and other public entities in Portugal which, in turn, is largely aligned with general tort liability rules. The chief purpose of this chapter to discuss and evaluate in practice the tortious liability of financial supervisors having regard of the institutional supervisory model adopted in Portugal, which includes the Bank of Portugal (Banco de Portugal), which is simultaneously the central bank and the financial supervisor for the banking sector, the Portuguese Insurance and Pension Funds Authority (Autoridade de Seguros e Fundos de Pensões), and the Portuguese Securities Market Commission (Comissão de Mercado de Valores Mobiliários).

title: The College Premium Rollercoaster and the Rebound of Lifetime Wage Growth: A Structural Analysis
affiliations: University of Quebec at Montreal (UQAM), York University - Faculty of Liberal Arts & Professional Studies, Le Mans University and University of Cergy-Pontoise

detail.title: The College Premium Rollercoaster and the Rebound of Lifetime Wage Growth: A Structural Analysis
detail.abstract: We develop a general-equilibrium OLG model of human capital to study the dynamics of the U.S. college premium and lifetime wage profiles between 1940 and 2020. The model features endogenous education and on-the-job training, along with exogenous aggregate (skill-neutral and skill-biased) shocks and cohort-specific trends in initial human capital endowments and learning capabilities. The estimated model replicates the W-shaped evolution of the college premium and the flattening then steepening of lifetime wage profiles. We show that changes in labor efficiency, rather than changes in relative skill prices, are the main driver of these dynamics. We quantify the contribution of estimated exogenous drivers and find a key role for the deterioration of human capital endowments and learning abilities among more recent cohorts. Crucially, endogenous adjustments in educational attainment and skill prices serve as powerful equalizing forces. Without these market mechanisms, the gap between the lifetime wage profiles of skilled and unskilled workers would widen and the college premium double.

title: The Regulation of Shareholder Democracy
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business, Bilkent University - Faculty of Business Administration, University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and University of Toronto

detail.title: The Regulation of Shareholder Democracy
detail.abstract: This paper studies how shareholder democracy regulations affect firm value and corporate decisions. We examine how investors and firms responded to an unexpected 2021 change in the SEC’s proxy guidelines that allowed more climate-related shareholder proposals. Firms with high carbon emissions experienced negative abnormal returns upon the announcement of the new guidelines. However, we find no evidence that high-emitting firms reduced actual or pledged carbon emissions or increased investment. We do find that high-emitting companies increased their engagement with proponents and stakeholders, suggesting that the new guidance diverted managerial attention toward non-operational activities. These findings question whether changes in SEC regulations of shareholder democracy enhance firm value and protect the welfare of investors.

title: Cover Crops a Potential Water Saver
affiliations: Statiunea de Cercetarte Dezvoltare pentru Viticultura si Vinificatie Bujoru, Statiunea de Cercetarte Dezvoltare pentru Viticultura si Vinificatie Bujoru, Statiunea de Cercetarte Dezvoltare pentru Viticultura si Vinificatie Bujoru, Statiunea de Cercetarte Dezvoltare pentru Viticultura si Vinificatie Bujoru and "Dunarea de Jos" University

detail.title: Cover Crops a Potential Water Saver
detail.abstract: This study investigates and evaluates the benefits brought by the use of cover crops in grapevine plantations and their impact on vegetative state as a result of increasing the amount of water present in the soil. Intensifying global warming phenomena has affected all ecosystems around the world, changing their specificity to new climate conditions. Due to extreme drought phenomena, the Balkan region is facing unprecedented water supply sortage, affecting both agricultural practices, including viticultural practices, and by default quality of life. The use of cover crops can become a viable choice for water resource conservation, assuring agricultural sustainability. Climate data, for 2024, analysis highlighted non-specific values for general and vine specific climate parameters. Due to extreme drought, cover crop experimental variants recorded limited vegetative growth and consequently had minimal effects on the soil water retention and vine plantation development. We aim at reestablishing experimental variants in the context of 2025 climate conditions, to obtain a positive impact regarding soil water reserves.

title: Sorting on Plan Design: Theory and Evidence from the ACA
affiliations: Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management, Wisconsin School of Business

detail.title: Sorting on Plan Design: Theory and Evidence from the ACA
detail.abstract: Health insurance plans differ in coverage levels and the combinations of cost-sharing attributes to achieve that level. I show that the proliferation of plan designs can result from asymmetric information. Though optimal risk protection requires concentrating coverage for larger losses via straight-deductibles, low-risk types sort into plans with more coverage for smaller losses to prevent pooling with the high-risk types. Consistent with the model, I show a large variation in plan designs exists in the ACA exchange and straight-deductible plans attract high-risk types. I calibrate the welfare effects of standardizing plan designs in the ACA.

title: Empirical Assessment of Pension Scheme and Economic Development in Nigeria
affiliations: University of Calabar, University of Calabar- Department of Banking & Finance, University of Calabar, Calabar Nigeria and University of Calabar, Calabar Nigeria

detail.title: Empirical Assessment of Pension Scheme and Economic Development in Nigeria
detail.abstract: Considering that the Pension Commission is an arena that provides some services that strengthen economic growth, the investigation analyzed the causal relationship between the value of the HDI and CPFAs, RRF, and TPF, assessing the role of pensions in Nigeria's economic development. Using the Ordinary Least Square model, the AES and RSA exert weak influence on the economy's gross domestic product, yet there is a strong empirical relationship between HDI and CPFAs, RRF, and TPF. The study recommended that retirement funds should be adequately monitored and deregulated, and the commission should operate without government abuse or interference. Additionally, since the stock of the Pension Commission exists within a macroeconomic environment, it is necessary for the institutional, political, and economic conditions to be conducive for the retirement fund to reach its full potential.

title: Ready To Switch? Fairness Implications from Heterogeneous Access to Climate-Friendly Substitutes
affiliations: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research

detail.title: Ready To Switch? Fairness Implications from Heterogeneous Access to Climate-Friendly Substitutes
detail.abstract: The decarbonization of residential heating and transport requires widespread adoption of climate-friendly technologies such as heat pumps and electric vehicles. As efforts to price emissions from these sectors ramp up, differences in the propensity and speed with which households switch to green substitutes will have immense distributional consequences. In this article, I argue that inequality in the 'capacity to switch' is central to the fairness of climate policy in consumer-focussed sectors. Importantly, such 'capacity to switch' is often constrained by factors outside the control of households, including market failures such as under-provision of transport infrastructure or split incentives in rented housing. I argue that fairness principles should be sensitive to these non-responsible factors. This would require abandoning fairness conceptions predicated on 'equality of outcome', such as vertical and horizontal equity, in favour of 'equality of opportunity' in reacting to carbon pricing. Building on luck-egalitarian theories of justice, I outline how such a fairness principle can be operationalised and tested empirically. The article concludes by showing how this perspective can inform the design of equitable climate policies.

reference: Submitted to Journal of Human Rights and the Environment
title: Climate Change and the Right to Education: A Twofold Relationship
affiliations: Middlesex University - Middlesex University Dubai and University of Cambridge - Department of Land Economy

detail.title: Climate Change and the Right to Education: A Twofold Relationship

publicationDetails.detailsText: Submitted to Journal of Human Rights and the Environment

detail.abstract: Climate change poses profound challenges to the protection and fulfilment of the right to education, both by directly disrupting access to schooling and by necessitating the transformation of curricula to equip learners for a climate-changed world. This article argues that the relationship between education and climate change is twofold: education must be shielded from climate disruption, and it must simultaneously serve as a tool of climate justice. Drawing on international, regional, and domestic jurisprudence, as well as the practice of human rights mechanisms, the article demonstrates how climate change impairs the availability and accessibility of education, particularly for displaced children and vulnerable communities, while also examining how education functions as an engine for sustainable development, intergenerational equity, and democratic resilience. Special attention is paid to recent advisory opinions of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, the International Court of Justice, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, which collectively affirm the normative content of States' climate obligations, examining their impact on the right to education. By situating education within evolving debates on extraterritorial obligations, curricular reform, and climate finance, the article contends that the right to education must be recognised as a constitutive element of climate governance. Far from being peripheral, education is both shield and sword: it must be protected against climate harm and mobilised to empower present and future generations to secure climate justice.

title: Foreign Direct Investment and Economic Growth in Nigeria: An ECM Approach
affiliations: University of Calabar, University of Calabar- Department of Banking & Finance and University of Calabar Banking and Finance

detail.title: Foreign Direct Investment and Economic Growth in Nigeria: An ECM Approach
detail.abstract: The study examined the impact of foreign direct investments (FDI) on economic growth, using annual data collected from CBN statistical bulletins over a period of 33 years (1988-2020). It specifically aimed to determine how FDI and related variables such as trade openness (OPEN), government size (GOVSIZE), and inflation rate (INF) influence Nigeria's economic growth. The data were analyzed using the ordinary least squares regression method after performing descriptive statistics, trend analysis, ADF unit root tests, and Johansen cointegration tests. The cointegration analysis results indicate that FDI, OPEN, GOVSIZE, and INF have long-term policy implications for Nigeria's economic growth. Supporting this, the study applied the error correction model to assess short-term effects. The findings show that FDI and trade openness positively impact economic growth, although trade openness was statistically insignificant. Conversely, government size and inflation rate negatively affect economic growth, with government size also being insignificant. Overall, the study concludes that FDI positively influences economic growth both in the short and long term. It is recommended that the government focus on attracting FDI through investor-friendly policies and implement programs aimed at promoting economic growth.

title: Global Plastic Waste Reallocation and Pollution: Evidence from China's Import Ban
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Real Estate, The University of Hong Kong and National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Global Plastic Waste Reallocation and Pollution: Evidence from China's Import Ban
detail.abstract: This paper examines the global spillover effects of China's 2017 plastic waste import ban, which abruptly disrupted the world's largest destination for plastic waste. Using monthly bilateral trade data and satellite-based PM 2.5 pollution measures from 2015 to 2023, we implement a difference-indifferences strategy to estimate the ban's impact on international waste flows and air quality in recipient countries. Approximately 50% of displaced waste was redirected to other Asian countries. In comparison to unaffected waste categories, the affected categories experienced a surge in monthly net imports of $1.088 million USD per average receiving country. The largest increases occurred in countries with limited recycling capacity and weak environmental governance, particularly from non-OECD exporters and countries with stricter environmental regulations. Areas near waste processing sites in highimport regions experienced higher PM 2.5 concentrations, suggesting notable environmental and health costs. These findings underscore the unintended consequences of unilateral environmental regulation and the need for coordinated global waste management.

title: Investigating Liquidity Creation in Nigerian Banks: A Study of United Bank for Africa
affiliations: University of Calabar- Department of Banking & Finance, University of Calabar (UNICAL), University of Calabar (UNICAL) and University of Uyo

detail.title: Investigating Liquidity Creation in Nigerian Banks: A Study of United Bank for Africa
detail.abstract: For the purpose of fostering economic expansion, enabling financial intermediation, assuring the efficient operation of markets, controlling risks, and preserving financial stability, banks' capacity to create and distribute liquidity is essential. This research assessed impact of liquidity creation on bank's performance. Using Ordinary Least Square model to analyse a time series of United Bank for Africa Plc from 2004-2021, findings reveals that the bank's ROA, ROE, and PBT had no significant correlation with the ratios of Cash and Due from Banks to Total Assets (CTTA), Impaired Loans to Gross Loans (ILTGL), Net Loans to Total Assets (NLTTA), or Loans Less Customer Deposits to Total Assets (CDTA). However, the bank's ROA, ROE, and PBT were significantly influenced by the Cost to Income ratio (COST) and Tier 1 Capital to Total Assets (T1TTA). It was suggested, among other things, that the phenomenon of Non-Performing Loans contributed to this outcome by lowering the performance of each bank's loan portfolio. Therefore, managers must devise measures to reduce non-performing loans. Banks should reduce the credit risk of their investments and maintain their liquidity primarily through their capital reserves (such as Tier 1 Capital).

title: Assessing Cross-Currency Predictability in Forex Markets: Insights from Limit Order Book Data
affiliations: , Lund University - Department of Economics and Stockholm University - Stockholm Business School

detail.title: Assessing Cross-Currency Predictability in Forex Markets: Insights from Limit Order Book Data
detail.abstract: Theoretical research suggests potential cross-currency predictability in currency exchange markets, but empirical findings with macro-based models show mixed results. This has led to a growing focus on micro-based models, which explore how trading integrates fundamental information into exchange rates. This study stands out by using detailed limit order book data for the foreign exchange market, enabling micro-level insights. It covers multiple currency pairs, assessing cross-currency predictability. Emphasizing short-term forecasts from 1 minute to 1 hour, it introduces factor-augmented regressions, including unsupervised and supervised principal components analysis to tackle data dimensionality, and contrasts those to LASSO and random forest methods. Our findings reveal generally low predictability across various models, supporting the Efficient Market Hypothesis. We find that cross-currency variables offer limited additional insight, but certain microstructure variables like order flow show short-term predictive power, suggesting transient market inefficiencies.

title:
Intro to Factor Investing 
DDA3600 - Factor Investing
affiliations: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen

detail.title:
Intro to Factor Investing 
DDA3600 - Factor Investing
detail.abstract: This lecture note is part of a course of The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen on Factor Investing (DDA3600), offering a comprehensive introduction to the theory and practice of factor-based asset pricing. This lecture provides a unified introduction to factor investing, a core methodology in quantitative investment and asset management. Starting from the foundational Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and its extension to multi-factor models, it explains how asset returns are driven by systematic risk factors and how anomalies arise when models fail to fully capture expected returns. The content bridges academic research and industry practice, covering key topics such as factor selection, model construction, performance attribution, risk management, and factor timing. The lecture highlights the evolution of factor investing, its empirical foundations, and practical applications, offering students a comprehensive framework for understanding and applying factor-based approaches in financial markets.

title: The Open Research Divide: A Comparative Analysis of Policy, Infrastructure, and Practice in North Africa
affiliations: Libyan Authority for Scientific Research

detail.title: The Open Research Divide: A Comparative Analysis of Policy, Infrastructure, and Practice in North Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I, Abulgasem Al Mashai, declare that there's no conflict of interest related to this study. The research was self-funded, and I have no personal or financial relationships with any people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced the outcomes or findings presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a comparative analysis of public data, including bibliometric information, national policies, and existing academic literature. It did not involve any direct research on human subjects, nor did it collect or use any personally identifiable information. Therefore, it falls outside the scope of review by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) and was conducted without the need for a formal ethics approval process.

detail.abstract: Objective: This study conducts a comparative analysis of the challenges and current state of open research-encompassing Open Access, Open Data, and Open Science-in five North African countries: Algeria, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, and Tunisia. It aims to dissect the systemic barriers hindering the region's equitable participation in the global knowledge ecosystem. Methods: A mixed-methods comparative approach was employed, integrating quantitative and qualitative data. The methodology includes bibliometric analysis of national journal platforms and databases like the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), statistical review of digital infrastructure indicators from the World Bank and ITU, and a systematic synthesis of national policies, institutional reports, and existing academic literature on researcher perceptions and challenges. Findings: The analysis reveals profound disparities across the region. While Egypt demonstrates high quantitative output through its national platform, it faces challenges in quality assurance and researcher capacity. Algeria exhibits a similar paradox of high volume but low international indexing. Tunisia shows progress through transformative agreements, whereas Morocco is developing its policy framework. Libya is in the nascent stages of building its digital research infrastructure. Overarching challenges include a significant digital and knowledge divide, inconsistent funding models, a lack of cohesive national policies, and persistent cultural barriers among researchers, such as negative perceptions of Open Access quality and language barriers. Conclusion: A one-size-fits-all strategy for promoting open research in North Africa is demonstrably ineffective. The region's heterogeneity demands context-specific, collaborative, and adequately funded strategies. Addressing systemic barriers related to infrastructure, policy, funding, and human capacity is essential to foster a truly open, equitable, and sustainable research ecosystem.

title: Original Peoples Count: The Resurgence of Indigenous Communities, Identities and Nations In Latin America
affiliations: Stanford University and Independent researcher

detail.title: Original Peoples Count: The Resurgence of Indigenous Communities, Identities and Nations In Latin America

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no financial or personal relationships that could have inappropriately influenced the work reported in this paper. This research was conducted without any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as potential conflicts of interest. Alberto Diaz-Cayeros is a Senior Fellow at the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law at Stanford University located on the ancestral and unceded lands of the Muwekma Ohlone peoples. Irma Alicia Velasquez Nimatuj is a Maya-K'iche' social anthropologist, journalist, and writer. declarations.ethicsApproval: Not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding.

detail.abstract: Latin American politics has undergone substantial transformation through the resurgence of Indigenous communities as political actors. This review examines Indigenous movements' evolution from social mobilization to institutional governance, analyzing how they captured political power in Bolivia and Ecuador while reshaping constitutional frameworks regionally.  Indigenous identity proves endogenous to political exclusion, with census data showing dramatic increases in self-identification linked to political empowerment. Approximately 58 million Indigenous peoples (9.8% of regional population) concentrate in 2,174 municipalities where they constitute majorities. Traditional governance institutions demonstrate superior democratic practices compared to conventional systems. Contemporary challenges include environmental criminalization of defenders, digital colonialism through AI knowledge extraction, and hybrid legal pluralism. Three research priorities emerge: historical trauma as determinant of political behavior; Indigenous health disparities as political barriers; and youth political participation in urban settings. Political science must incorporate Indigenous epistemologies and recognize these communities as engines of democratic innovation.

title: Nonlinear Thresholds and Structural Determinants of Climate-Related Emigration: A Machine Learning Approach
affiliations: "Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iasi, RO

detail.title: Nonlinear Thresholds and Structural Determinants of Climate-Related Emigration: A Machine Learning Approach
detail.abstract: This study investigates nonlinear links between climate and international migration using global panel data (1960-2020) aggregated by decade. A machine-learning framework based on Random Forests, complemented by generalized additive models (GAMs), partial dependence plots (PDPs), and SHAP values, is used to detect climatic thresholds and structural moderation. Random-Forest variable importance indicates that structural conditions-especially infrastructure quality and agrarian structuredominate predictive power, while temperature and precipitation contribute additional, nonlinear signal. GAM and PDP/ICE profiles uncover a thermal threshold around 25-27°C and a non-escalating hot tail above about 29°C, consistent with capacity constraints in highly exposed contexts. Precipitation exhibits a hump-shaped relationship, with effects concentrated at moderate rainfall bands (roughly 150-220 mm per month). Results are robust across specifications and over time and are consistent across income-based subsamples (median split), underscoring that climate operates as a conditional rather than autonomous driver of migration. Recognizing these nonlinear thresholds and the role of structural capacity is essential for anticipating climate-related mobility and immobility under continued warming.

title: Foliar Urea and Nano Urea Applications: Impacts on Growth, Chlorophyll Content, Yield Attributes and Economics of Wheat (Triticum Aestivum L.)
affiliations: Independent, Independent, Independent and Independent

detail.title: Foliar Urea and Nano Urea Applications: Impacts on Growth, Chlorophyll Content, Yield Attributes and Economics of Wheat (Triticum Aestivum L.)
detail.abstract: Wheat, a vital staple cereal crop feeding a large share of the global population, requires efficient nutrient management; however, limited comparative research has evaluated the physiological, agronomic and economic impacts of foliar-applied conventional urea and nano urea under field conditions. To address this issue, a study was conducted during the rabi season of 2023-2024 at the Instructional Farm, Post Graduate Institute, Mahatma Phule Krishi Vidyapeeth, Rahuri, with a view to study the "Response of foliar application of urea and nano urea on yield and nutrient uptake of wheat under irrigated condition". The experiment was conducted in randomized block design and treatments were consisted of 12 levels of nutrient combination with 3 replications. The application of the general recommended dose of fertilizers (GRDF) at 120:60:40 kg N:P2O5:K2O with 10 tons of farmyard manure (FYM) per hectare yielded the most beneficial results for the wheat crop. This treatment resulted in the highest significant values for plant population, chlorophyll content, and yield contributing characters, including the length of the ear, number of spikelets and grains per ear, and grain weight. Economically, the GRDF treatment also provided the highest gross monetary returns (113,955 ₹ ha-1), net monetary returns (64,801 ₹ ha-1), and B-C ratio of 2.32. However, the study concluded that treatments involving 75% of the recommended nitrogen dose applied to the soil, combined with a 4% or 6% foliar spray of urea, performed on par with the GRDF treatment. This suggests a potential to save 25% of the nitrogen fertilizer for wheat while achieving comparable results.

title: What Does It Take? Quantifying Cross-Country Transfers in the Eurozone
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, , Stanford University and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: What Does It Take? Quantifying Cross-Country Transfers in the Eurozone
detail.abstract: We compute the cross-country transfers that result from unconventional monetary policy in the Eurozone. The ECB funds the expansion of its aggregate balance sheet mostly by issuing bank reserves and cash in core countries. The national central banks (NCBs) in periphery countries then borrow from the core NCBs at below-market rates to fund the asset purchases and bank lending. In addition, NCBs in the periphery lend more to their own banks at below-market rates. To compute the cross-country transfers, we compare the resulting cross-country distribution of NCB income to a counterfactual scenario without the ECB and without non-marketable intra-Eurozone debt. We document significant and persistent transfers from the core to the periphery.

title: Health Financing and Humah Development in Sub Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Experience
affiliations: University of Calabar, Calabar Nigeria, University of Calabar, University of Calabar- Department of Banking & Finance and University of Calabar (UNICAL)

detail.title: Health Financing and Humah Development in Sub Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Experience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest

detail.abstract: This study examines how Nigeria's economic growth is influenced by health financing. Its goals were to determine the effect of government recurrent spending on health and economic growth in Nigeria, as well as the relationship between government capital expenditure and health spending. The study used time series data from 1990 to 2022 and adopted an ex post facto research design. Ordinary least squares (OLS) was used for data analysis. The conclusion was that there is no significant correlation between Nigeria's economic growth and government capital spending on health. Further analysis showed that Nigeria's economic growth and government recurrent health spending do not have a strong relationship. To promote sustainable economic growth, it is recommended that the government increase its budget allocation to the health sector. Additionally, the government should ensure timely payment of health workers' salaries, wages, and benefits, which can motivate them to work more efficiently and increase per capita income.

title: Curb Staging: Understanding the Impacts of Automated Vehicle Ridehail Fleet Operations Under Different Parking Policies
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Institute of Transportation Studies, University of California, Irvine, UC Berkeley, UC Berkeley and UC Berkeley

detail.title: Curb Staging: Understanding the Impacts of Automated Vehicle Ridehail Fleet Operations Under Different Parking Policies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The research was funded, in part, by Waymo.
declarations.funderStatement: The research was funded, in part, by Waymo.

detail.abstract: Automated vehicle (AV) ridehailing services are now operating in several metropolitan regions in the United States. While providing benefits, AV ridehailing services may exacerbate issues related to curb usage and vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT) in urban areas. The objective of this study is to provide guidance to cities by evaluating the impacts of AVs' short-term curb usage for staging between serving ride requests. We focus on the following performance metrics: VKT, curb productivity, customer wait time, and customer matching rate. To perform the analysis, we use a high-fidelity commercial simulation tool that models the dynamics of AV ridehailing fleet operations. We use high-quality, high-resolution data, including synthetic ridehailing trip data and forecasts of curb availability. Our baseline scenario includes a hypothetical fleet size of 1,700 vehicles serving a hypothetical total of 68,000 daily trips in San Francisco, California. We construct scenarios that vary in terms of whether, where, and when AVs can stage at curbs, as well as whether AVs strategically reposition to high-demand areas. We also vary the day of the week. According to our simulation results, excluding AVs from staging at the curb would increase daily VKT by over 200,000 kilometers or nearly 60 percent, compared to scenarios where AVs can stage at the curb. In a separate analysis, we find that prohibiting curb staging in residential areas and on curbsides with metered parking would increase empty VKT by 5.4%. We also present key performance metrics that are both temporally and spatially resolved, providing additional policy-relevant information. The simulation modeling is supplemented by expert interviews (n=14) with practitioners, regulators, and policymakers in the fields of curbside management and innovative mobility to gain additional insight on policy considerations related to AV curb access, staging, and parking.

title: Long-Term Exchange Rate Pass-Through to Prices
affiliations: Bank of Russia, Bank of Russia and Bank of Russia

detail.title: Long-Term Exchange Rate Pass-Through to Prices
detail.abstract: Empirical research shows that the short-term exchange rate pass-through to prices is quite small. However, can we extrapolate this conclusion to the long term? Our research suggests that the long-term exchange rate pass-through to prices is close to complete. We show this using the Bayesian method to estimate the static general equilibrium model with two effects of real price rigidity: the effect of distribution costs for tradable goods and the ad hoc capture of market share effect. The innovation to the empirical estimation of the model is that it is based on the long-term data for 2012-2018 and is performed in two stages. At the first stage, the intensity of the distribution cost effect is estimated on the statistics for 80 regions of Russia. At the second stage, we estimate elasticity parameters that allow us to calculate the long-term exchange rate pass-through to prices. The total exchange rate pass-through turns out to be almost complete and amounts in, for the basic specification, to 98.5% in the long term (more than five years).

title: Disagreement Amon Institutional Investors and Expected Returns
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU)

detail.title: Disagreement Amon Institutional Investors and Expected Returns
detail.abstract: This paper aims to reverse-engineer investors' subjective expectations about the future distribution of asset prices from their portfolio holdings. Following a tradition in the literature, I assume frictions are akin to implicit investment taxes and quantify the "wedges" in beliefsor implicit taxes on returns-that explain the observed deviations in holdings from a modelimplied diversified portfolio. As a first application, I demonstrate that the dispersion in investors' beliefs positively predicts cross-section of asset returns, consistent with the presence of asymmetric information among investors. Furthermore, I aim to test whether these quantifiable private information held by investors explain part of the residual in the crosssection of returns left unexplained by known characteristics. Preliminary results support this, indicating that the market may not fully incorporate "who owns what" as a relevant piece of information-an unexpected outcome for a competitive market with revealed actions.

title: Behavioral Responses to Time-Varying Congestion Pricing: A Natural Experiment from New York City
affiliations: Northeastern University (USA)

detail.title: Behavioral Responses to Time-Varying Congestion Pricing: A Natural Experiment from New York City
detail.abstract: We provide the first causal evidence that congestion pricing induces asymmetric temporal substitution exclusively at specific pricing boundaries. Using New York City's January 2025 implementation and high-frequency establishment-level mobility data, we employ a Differencein-Discontinuities design testing multiple potential thresholds. We find a statistically significant 5.75% temporal shift only at the 5AM weekday boundary (p < 0.05), with precisely estimated null effects at all other transitions including both weekend boundaries. This sharp concentration at a single threshold robust to bandwidth selection and alternative control cities reveals that temporal substitution requires precise alignment between pricing boundaries and latent schedule flexibility. Despite limited behavioral change at only one of four pricing boundaries, non-linear traffic flow relationships translate this 5.75% shift into substantial congestion relief. These findings challenge standard congestion pricing models that assume symmetric schedule delay costs and suggest that program effectiveness depends primarily on trip elimination and modal substitution rather than temporal redistribution.

title: Monetary Policy under Global Scrutiny: A Credibility -Responsive Framework for Financially Open Economies

detail.title: Monetary Policy under Global Scrutiny: A Credibility -Responsive Framework for Financially Open Economies

publicationDetails.detailsText: The paper has not appeared yet.

detail.abstract: This article proposes a credibility-responsive monetary policy (CRMP) framework for central banks in financially open economies. Building on the Portfolio Theory of Inflation (Bossone, 2025), it treats credibility as an endogenous, priced constraint that evolves with investor perceptions and policy conduct. Unlike conventional models that assume fixed credibility or neglect capital market dynamics, CRMP embeds investor beliefs into the transmission mechanism and adapts standard policy rules accordingly. The framework explains why identical shocks can yield divergent outcomes across countries, depending on how global investors assess policy commitment. Its mechanics are illustrated through a two-country simulation, with preliminary empirical support from a synthetic credibility index. CRMP provides policymakers with diagnostic and operational tools for navigating volatile capital markets, anchoring expectations, and preserving macroeconomic space under global scrutiny.

title: Optimal Multi-Period Dynamic Portfolios for Sustainable Investing
affiliations: East China Normal University (ECNU), Peking University and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Optimal Multi-Period Dynamic Portfolios for Sustainable Investing
detail.abstract: Sustainable investing involves balancing traditional investment strategies with environmental, social, and governance-related (ESG) objectives to improve long-term outcomes. We develop a stochastic control framework for constructing optimal multi-period dynamic ESG portfolios, in which investors form dynamic portfolios by maximizing utility functions that account for both profitability and the average ESG scores of their portfolios in the near and distant future. We provide an explicit solution to the investors' utility maximization problem, and show that the optimal weight is a linear combination of three components: a financial performance component, an ESG component, and a component reflecting the weight from the previous period. Using the U.S. stock market data, we find that the multi-period dynamic ESG portfolio outperforms single-period portfolios in terms of Sharpe ratios, alphas, and ESG scores. Our article extends the dynamic portfolio theory in the context of sustainable investing, and provides guidance to practitioners on tailoring ESG portfolios to their specific preferences and to market conditions related to ESG.

title: Long-term Capital Market Assumptions
affiliations: The University of Western Australia, Monash University - Monash Centre for Financial Studies and Monash University - Monash Centre for Financial Studies

detail.title: Long-term Capital Market Assumptions
detail.abstract: In today's volatile financial landscape, the need for accurate and adaptable investment strategies has never been greater. Capital market assumptions (CMAs) form the foundation of long-term asset allocation, providing investors with essential estimates of expected returns, volatility, and risk correlations across asset classes. This study aims to develop our CMAs for both equity and fixed income, outlining the expected returns, and volatility estimates in various countries/regions. We employ rigorous backtesting to evaluate various forecasting models and find that in many cases, less complicated models outshine their more sophisticated counterparts. The cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio outperforms more complex models in 15 out of 20 equity indexes. For Treasury bonds, U.S. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), and corporate bonds, we show that current bond yields serve as reliable predictors of future returns. However, our model for T-bills demonstrates superior accuracy over the Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF), with lower RMSE, and MAE values. The effects of inflation and foreign exchange rate changes are also considered to account for nominal price changes and cross-border investment.

title: Mean-Variance Strikes Back: Reassessing the 1/N Diversification Superiority
affiliations: University of Agder - School of Business and Law

detail.title: Mean-Variance Strikes Back: Reassessing the 1/N Diversification Superiority
detail.abstract: Equal weighting is often seen as the ultimate benchmark: simple, robust, and, according to DeMiguel, Garlappi, and Uppal (2009), superior to mean-variance optimization out of sample. This view has shaped both academic research and industry practice. We challenge it.
