title: The Rousseau-Portalis Doctrine: French Legal Thought and the Law of War – Parts I and II
affiliations: George Washington University - Law School

detail.title: The Rousseau-Portalis Doctrine: French Legal Thought and the Law of War – Parts I and II

publicationDetails.detailsText: Lieber Institute for Law & Warfare, Articles of War (USMA)

detail.abstract: The Rousseau-Portalis Doctrine is the idea that war is a relationship between states rather than individuals and, accordingly, military operations must be conducted exclusively against the enemy forces and not against civilians who do not take an active part in hostilities. Grounded in Grotian thought but enhanced and refined by Enlightenment thinkers, this revolutionary idea has had a significant impact on the law of war over the past two centuries. The doctrine is understood today as a salient component in the undergirding framework of the law of war. This is a two-part series illustrating the impact of French legal thought on the formation of the law of war with a specific focus on the Rousseau-Portalis Doctrine. The first part provides a brief background on Jean-Jacques Rousseau and Jean-Étienne-Marie Portalis, their views on the law of nations, and their ideas that form the substance of the Rousseau-Portalis Doctrine. The second part traces the evolution of that doctrine and discusses its impact on the law of war.

title: Do New Products Affect a Company’s Share Price? An Event Study of Apple

detail.title: Do New Products Affect a Company’s Share Price? An Event Study of Apple
detail.abstract:
This study investigates the relationship between Apple’s stock price movement and its new product announcements from 2020 to 2024. As a dominant force in the global technology sector, Apple’s innovations such as the M series chips and Vision Pro consistently attract consumer interest and media attention, impacting global financial markets and investor sentiment. The study aims to address several key questions: firstly, whether Apple’s stock exhibits a discernible trend on the day of its new product releases; secondly, what patterns emerge in its stock price behaviour over the subsequent two or three days following these announcements; and thirdly, how these announcements influence Apple’s stock performance over the subsequent 12 months. Employing event study methodology, the analysis uses daily adjusted closing prices from the National Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotations (NASDAQ) through Python. Events are defined, including major announcements like the Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC)[1] and Wanderlust events[2], gathered directly from Apple’s official website. The study calculates indicators such as Abnormal Return (AR), Cumulative Abnormal Return (CAR), Average Abnormal Return (AAR), and Cumulative Average Abnormal Return (CAAR) to research the impact of these events on Apple’s stock price. Findings suggest an initial decline in stock price post-announcement, especially for stock prices related to innovative products followed by a recovery period and potential long-term growth in the subsequent 12 months, providing advice to investors, analysts, and manufacturers within Apple’s supply chain. By investigating the differences between the short term and the long term, this study offers stock price reactions to new product announcement events, supporting strategic decision-making in investment and supply chain management practices.


[1] The Apple Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC) is an annual event hosted by Apple Inc. where developers can attend sessions and labs with Apple engineers, and preview upcoming updates to the company's software platforms, including iOS, macOS, iPadOS, and watchOS.

[2] The Apple Wanderlust event is a marketing keynote presentation by Apple Inc., typically held in September, where the company unveils its latest products and technologies, including new models of iPhones, Apple Watches, and other hardware and software updates.

title: Violation and Enforcement of Workplace Regulations: Evidence from Mexican Firm Inspections
affiliations: University of Zurich - Department of Economics, Banco de México and University of Zurich - Department of Economics

detail.title: Violation and Enforcement of Workplace Regulations: Evidence from Mexican Firm Inspections
detail.abstract: This paper studies the characteristics of large formal firms that violate workplace regulations and analyzes how regulatory enforcement affects firms and workers. A stylized model of monopsonistic firms - in which employers set both wages and working conditions - shows that high levels of labor market power can lead to violations in workplace regulations, and that the enforcement of such regulations can raise firm employment through an expansion of labor supply. To test the model's predictions, we use administrative records of stratified random firm inspections in Mexico, which enforce compliance with workplace safety, health regulations, and mandatory worker training. We link these records to panel surveys and administrative employer-employee data for large manufacturing firms. We find that firms are more likely to be found violating regulations if they invest less in worker training, have lower productivity, employ a smaller share of women, and employ a larger share of the local labor market. Furthermore, inspections tend to increase regulatory compliance, reflected in greater investment in worker training, fewer workplace accidents, and a lower likelihood of future violations. Using a staggered difference-indifferences design, we estimate that inspections increase firm employment by 4 to 7% within one year. Average firm wages decrease by less than 2%, driven by changes in worker composition rather than changes in individual wage setting. Our results indicate that enforcing workplace regulations in large manufacturing firms can be an effective policy tool for improving working conditions, mitigating labor market power, and simultaneously increasing firm employment.

title: Sustainable Investment Management in India
affiliations: ANU College of Law

detail.title: Sustainable Investment Management in India
detail.abstract: While ESG investing has gained traction in India, concerns of greenwashing also became important, thus giving rise to regulations attempting to tackle this. However, the interest in ESG investing seems to have dipped since 2021. This article will survey both the state of play and the regulatory landscape around ESG investing with a focus on fund managers. Specifically, it examines the regulations for mutual funds and asset managers that have ESG offerings issued in 2023 and regulations for credit rating agencies with regard to ESG ratings. These regulations have been issued by India's market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and sit alongside preexisting regulations for fund managers. Since the 2023 regulations direct ESG funds to ensure that their investments are in companies which comply with the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting requirements, this article will also examine the BRSR requirements and their lack of comparability with similar disclosure requirements internationally. Some earlier case law on the duties of fund managers will also be explored to facilitate analysis on how ESG requirements might be enforced. The article will argue that alongside effective regulation, investor education and publicity of regulatory compliance or lack of it will also be important if the nascent market for ESG investing is to develop in the country.

title: Тhe Impact of Local Government in Local Development with Particular Emphasis on the Republic of Macedonia
affiliations: , FON University and FON University

detail.title: Тhe Impact of Local Government in Local Development with Particular Emphasis on the Republic of Macedonia
detail.abstract: Local Economic Development (LED) is a process by which the local government cooperates with public and private institutions to create favorable conditions for economic and social development. It focuses on the existing resources, such as access to various activities at the local and regional level to provide economic and social welfare, better living standards as well as reducing the unemployment and poverty. The impact of local economic development in the region primarily is determined by national factors, of the central government, such as national development policies, the security situation in the country and the region, the country's geostrategic position, macroeconomic policy, fiscal policy, financial policy and the development of market economy. The local authorities, depending on the level of their fiscal autonomy, financial capacity, administrative capacity, the geographical position of the unit of local government, natural resources, municipal infrastructure, the educational structure of people, may significantly affect the promotion of their region to attract international and local investment to support the new and existing enterprises by creating conditions for business development, increased employment, improved living conditions, increase municipal budget revenues derived from business and other incomes. The aim of this study is not only to survey the rural and local development, but to analyze the impact of functional and fiscal decentralization in supporting and promoting the local and regional economic development in the Republic of Macedonia.

title: Principles of AI for Investment Management From Calculation to Cognition
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Principles of AI for Investment Management From Calculation to Cognition

detail.abstract: Recent advances in AI, in particular large language models and cognitive architectures, are driving a paradigm shift in investment management. While traditional, calculation-centric approaches that rely on historical price patterns struggle with the causal, contextual and non-stationary nature of markets. This paper argues for a cognition-first approach: AI systems that ingest real-time information, model expectations and surprise, surface causal pathways, and deliver interpretable decision support to human investors. We present a set of core principles for designing and deploying these systems, emphasizing information flow, expectations, materiality, human-AI synergy, interpretability, and recommend governance and evaluation approaches that make cognitive AI suitable for fiduciary use.

title: Fiscal Drag in Theory and in Practice: a European Perspective
affiliations: Banco de España, European Central Bank (ECB), Bank of Portugal, University of Essex, Catholic University of Milan, Central Bank of Malta, Central Bank of Ireland, Latvijas Banka, Banque de France, National Bank of Belgium, Bank of Italy, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Banco de España, Banco de España, Ifo Institute, Latvijas Banka, Bank of Greece, Banque Centrale du Luxembourg, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, De Nederlandsche Bank, VU University Amsterdam, Central Bank of Ireland, Oesterreichische Nationalbank (OeNB), National Bank of Slovakia, , Banco de España, Bank of Slovenia, Banque de France, Banka Slovenije, Bank of Lithuania, Bank of Greece - Economic Research Department and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Fiscal Drag in Theory and in Practice: a European Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive characterization of “fiscal drag”—the increase in tax revenue that occurs when nominal tax bases grow but nominal parameters of progressive tax legislation are not updated accordingly—across 21 European countries using a microsimulation approach. First, we estimate tax-to-base elasticities, showing that the progressivity built in each country’s personal income tax system induces elas- ticities around 1.7–1.9 for many countries, indicating a potential for large fiscal drag effects. We unpack these elasticities to show stark heterogeneity in their underlying mechanisms (tax brackets or tax deductions and credits), across income sources (labor, capital, self-employment, public benefits), and across the individual income distribu- tion. Second, we extend the analysis beyond these elasticities to study fiscal drag in practice between 2019 and 2023, incorporating observed income growth and legislative changes. We quantify the actual impact of fiscal drag and the extent to which govern- ment policies have offset it, either through indexation or other reforms. Our results provide new insights into the fiscal and distributional effects of fiscal drag in Europe, as well as useful statistics for modeling public finances.

title: Nest Quest ROI: An Ethical, Asset-Backed Financial System

detail.title: Nest Quest ROI: An Ethical, Asset-Backed Financial System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This work is an independent research initiative conducted under SoftTelRG LLC.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research did not involve human participants or experimental subjects requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was entirely self-funded by the author through SoftTelRG LLC, with no external funding or institutional grants.

detail.abstract:
This article introduces Nest Quest ROI, a research-grade book and simulation engine developed to test whether transparent, asset-backed models can yield fairer and more resilient outcomes than conventional debt-based finance. The framework is grounded in four principles: prohibition of unjust value transfer, elimination of harmful uncertainty, primacy of real asset value, and alignment of incentives through risk-sharing.

The engine operationalizes these principles through a live simulation platform, new evaluation metrics such as the Real Net Interest Margin (RNIM) and Equity Return on Asset (ERA), and an inflation-resilient savings mechanism—the Digital Gold Savings Account (DGSA). While conventional banks assess profitability through Net Interest Margin (NIM), RNIM is introduced as a comparative measure, recalibrated to reflect real, asset-linked income flows in a debt-free framework.

By making assumptions explicit, reproducible, and auditable, Nest Quest ROI offers households, investors, and institutions a transparent method to test scenarios under identical conditions. The framework is designed to align with ethical finance principles that emphasize fairness, shared risk, and asset-backing. This article invites economists, ethicists, policymakers, and financial institutions to critique the architecture, test the claims, and refine the model for broader adoption.

title: Precise Prediction on the Corrosion Prevention Ability of 1,2,4-Triazole Derivatives: An Artificial Neural Network Approach

detail.title: Precise Prediction on the Corrosion Prevention Ability of 1,2,4-Triazole Derivatives: An Artificial Neural Network Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

keywords: Artificial neural network (ANN) ES Energy & Environment

detail.abstract: Corrosion can have a significant impact, including the leaking of hazardous substances into the environment and damaging technological devices, which can impair ecosystems and cause pollution. Establishing new methods to prevent corrosion promotes environmental sustainability. Corrosion inhibitors minimize material waste, prolong material life, and minimize environmental pollution, with the initiatives for waste optimization of industrial processes. Quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) with the artificial neural network (ANN) can assist inventory optimization by quickly identifying new corrosion inhibitor compounds, which leads to economically profitable for the end users. Early studies explained the inhibitory effectiveness (IE) and the molecule's quantum characteristics were related, and a process was developed to establish a potential non-linear equation between corrosion inhibitors' experimental inhibition efficiency (IE exp) and specific quantum parameters for 1,2,4-Triazole derivatives. The current work aims to compare the prediction of non-linear models from the previous study and ANN used in this study. According to the research, the ANN predicts inhibition efficiencies more accurately and efficiently than the non-linear model, where correlation coefficient R (between IE exp and calculated inhibition efficiency (IE calc) increased from 0.888 to 0.967 and mean square error decreased from 4.33×10-4 to 9.81×10-5 respectively. This study summarizes the application of ANN to overcome non-linear problems.

title: Are Physicians' Motivations Stable Over Time? An Investigation before, During, and after a Pandemic
affiliations: Danish Centre for Health Economics - DaCHE, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Aarhus University and Danish Centre for Health Economics - DaCHE

detail.title: Are Physicians' Motivations Stable Over Time? An Investigation before, During, and after a Pandemic

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No declaration of interest
declarations.funderStatement: Financial support of the Carlsberg Foundation [Grant number CF22-0474] and the Novo Nordisk Foundation [Grant number: NNF18OC0033978].

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Southern Denmark, DaCHE Discussion Papers, Bind 2025, Nr. 1.

detail.abstract: Many healthcare systems struggle with recruitment and retention of physicians for specific specialities or in certain locations. One solution may be to design policies that appeal to their work motivations. Recent studies show that physicians' motivations vary and also link with their behaviour. However, little is known about whether physicians' motivations are stable over time. We exploit a major shock to physicians' working conditions to investigate stability in their motivations. Using unique survey data on a balanced panel of 448 general practitioners (GPs) in Denmark, this study examines GPs' motivations before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. We examine GPs' intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, user orientation, and public service motivation to capture both their self-centred and pro-social motivations. A series of fixed effects and quantile regression models show that each type of motivation follows a distinct pattern with regards to the timing and direction of changes during the study period. However, across all motivations the magnitude of these changes appears small. Subgroup analyses suggest that older GPs and male GPs exhibit higher stability in some motivations, and that practice and area characteristics do not affect motivation trends. Our results support that physicians' motivations are fairly stable overall and thereby may serve as useful inputs to policy design. Policymakers can thus better align the goals of the healthcare system with those of its workers, serving to promote a more sustainable and productive healthcare workforce.

title: Decentralization And Financing of Primary and Secondary Education in the Republic of Macedonia
affiliations: and

detail.title: Decentralization And Financing of Primary and Secondary Education in the Republic of Macedonia
detail.abstract: The main aim of the process of Decentralization of education was to improve conditions, quality educational standards and to enable access to education. However, in order the process of decentralization of education to achieve its objectives, is necessary to be accompanied by sufficient fiscal decentralization, sufficient funding versus authorizations by the Local authorities in the sphere of education, exacerbates the efficiency of providing public services. The main aim of this paper is to analyze the theoretical and empirical analysis of the forms of financing of primary and secondary education in the Republic of Macedonia in the time period from the beginning of the process of decentralization since 2005. The paper includes a review of the financial sufficiency for the realization of this comity, the criteria on the basis of which the funds from the central government to the local government are distributed and the criteria for determining the level of education budget at the local level. A number of problems have been identified in the application of current methods and an alternative approach to estimate the cost for student needs has been proposed. In order to make an informed decision about the required levels of resources, research needs to be done to determine the costs associated with the education of students with different levels of need.

title: From Data to Awakening: A Seven-Level Typology of Transformative Research Outcomes

detail.title: From Data to Awakening: A Seven-Level Typology of Transformative Research Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This paper introduces a seven-level typology of research results-descriptive, interpretative, prescriptive, reflective, generative, transformative, and meta-transformative-offering a dynamic framework for understanding scholarly depth and impact. Fluid and interconnected, these levels guide inquiry from observation to societal transformation. The typology bridges empirical insight and conceptual depth, helping scholars integrate data with meaning and purpose. It is especially relevant to community-based and visionary studies. Applications in sustainability, education, and health show how research evolves into transformative practice. Framing inquiry as a recursive and sacred endeavor, this model affirms research's potential to illuminate truths, empower communities, and awaken new possibilities across disciplines and cultures.

title: Better Labor Market Options Reduce Workplace Injuries

detail.title: Better Labor Market Options Reduce Workplace Injuries

declarations.ethicsApproval: IRB approval was obtained via the University of California, the University of Pennsylvania, and the Committee for the Protection of Human Subjects (CPHS) in the California Health and Human Services division (CalHHS).
declarations.funderStatement: R. Jisung Park acknowledges grant funding from the Russell Sage Foundation and the Washington Center for Equitable Growth.

detail.abstract: When workers' labor market outside options improve, their wages go up. What about other non-wage amenities? Using a Bartik shift-share IV that isolates shocks to workers' outside options in the labor market, we find that better labor market options meaningfully reduce the workplace injury rate: a one-standard-deviation improvement in outside options lowers injuries by about 0.18 standard deviations. These results suggest that external labor market conditions influence incentives to maintain safe workplaces, which has important implications for designing public policy, including those that regulate workplace health and safety and alter labor market competition.

title: United States White Victim Homicide Clearance
affiliations: Northeastern University, Institute for Security and Public Policy at the School of Criminology and Criminal Justice

detail.title: United States White Victim Homicide Clearance
detail.abstract:
In order to look at United States homicide clearance since the FBI started issuing annual Supplementary Homicide Reports (SHRs) in 1976, a dataset has been created of all cleared (race-identified), A-type (murder and non-negligent manslaughter) homicides, not including negligent (CIR code 50 series) and justified (CIR code 80 series) homicides.  This dataset has 692,604 records, each with 28 fields, so 19.4 million cell values.

It is used to examine the matrix of the four race categories of black and white lead offenders and victims – B-B, B-W, W-B, and W-W(setting aside the 3.2% of cleared homicides involving other races) – with the four homicide situation categories Solo vs. Solo, Solo vs. Multiple, Multiple vs. Solo, and Multiple vs. Multiple.

The reason for this is to see whether extra (non-lead) defendants in the “Multiple” offender cases are distributed in a race neutral fashion. More specifically, special attention is focused on the white victim cases and the state-by-state records of extra defendants in B-W versus W-W cases. An Appendix summarizes all the dataset variables (counts) for each state.

title: The Evolution of Slavery: From Physical Chains to Economic Systems of Control
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Evolution of Slavery: From Physical Chains to Economic Systems of Control

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could inappropriately influence or bias the content of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects; therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive any external funding.

detail.abstract: Slavery is widely believed to be a historical relic, abolished centuries ago. Yet, its structural logic persists in modern society under subtler forms. Instead of chains and whips, today's systems rely on wages, debt, taxation, and consumerism to maintain cycles of dependency. Workers often believe they are free because they can choose their occupation, city, or lifestyle, but when survival demands endless labor, freedom becomes an illusion. This paper explores the parallels between traditional slavery and contemporary economic structures, examining how debt, the 9-to-5 work cycle, inflation, and consumer culture function as mechanisms of control. Unlike historical slaves who recognized their bondage, modern workers are often unaware of the invisible chains constraining their lives. The study concludes with pathways to liberation: shifting from wages to assets, leveraging knowledge, escaping the debt trap, reforming education, and applying Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability, and Learning (MEAL) frameworks to redesign systems. True freedom, the paper argues, is not measured by paychecks, but by ownership, knowledge, and the ability to create enduring value beyond mere survival.

title: No Means No: A Critique of the 'Feeble No' Doctrine in Mahmood Farooqui v. State
affiliations: Kurukshetra University

detail.title: No Means No: A Critique of the 'Feeble No' Doctrine in Mahmood Farooqui v. State

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N.A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N.A
declarations.funderStatement: N.A

detail.abstract: The foundation of sexual assault jurisprudence is consent, which sets legal intimacy apart from violent crimes. Judicial interpretation has frequently failed due to patriarchal presumptions, even though the 2013 revisions to Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code made it clear that consent must be voluntary, explicit, and revocable. In Mahmood Farooqui v. State (2017), the Delhi High Court's ruling that a "feeble no" can infer permission dangerously breaches the lines between autonomy and statutory rights for survivors. This essay examines the "feeble no" doctrine, placing the decision within the context of India's developing consent jurisprudence and using State v. Norman (USA, 1991) and R v. Olugboja (UK, 1981) as points of comparison. It draws attention to the legal and social repercussions of misinterpreting consent through doctrinal analysis, feminist critique, and comparative study. The paper argues for a reaffirmation of affirmative consent standards to ensure gender justice and safeguard women's dignity and autonomy.

title: The Impact of Active Labour Policies on Economic Growth
affiliations: AAB College - Faculty of Economics, , Universiteti AAB and AAB College

detail.title: The Impact of Active Labour Policies on Economic Growth
detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the mechanisms of active labour market policy in the case of Kosovo and the impact on reducing the unemployment rate and increasing employment. This research is descriptive, analytic, and exploratory. The data used are secondary data in the quarter for the period 2016-2020, which are provided by the Kosovo Agency of Statistics. The study uses the OLS (ordinary least square) econometric model and Pearson correlation in order to assess the impact of unemployment and employment rate on Kosovo's GDP (gross domestic product). The paper concludes that Kosovo has approved a large number of programs for the activation of the unemployed, mainly young people, but generally young university graduates are in a higher structure and rate in the composition of the unemployment rate. It is generally accepted that university graduates as workforce are the key driver of economic growth and development (Ziberi, Rexha, & Ukshini, 2021). This allows us to come up with further recommendations, such as the active policies in labour market in the case of Kosovo to be designed in the future based on a costbenefit perspective and in order to measure their effectiveness.

title: A Choice-Based Approach to the Measurement of Inflation Expectations
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank,  and Heidelberg University - Alfred Weber Institute for Economics

detail.title: A Choice-Based Approach to the Measurement of Inflation Expectations
detail.abstract: Economists widely rely on measures of inflation expectations and uncertainty elicited via density forecasts. This method, where respondents assign probabilities to pre-specified ranges, has been subjected to criticism particularly in the recent times of high and volatile inflation. We propose a new method to elicit the full distribution of inflation expectations, which is rooted in decision theory and can be implemented in standard surveys. In two large surveys and one laboratory experiment, we demonstrate that it leads to well-defined expectations that fulfil both subjective and objective quality criteria. The method is neither perceived as more difficult nor does it take more time to complete compared to the current standard. In contrast to density forecasts, the method is robust to differences in the state of the economy and thus allows comparisons across time and across countries. The method is portable and can be applied to elicit different macroeconomic expectations.

title: The European Single Market and Intra-EU Trade: An Assessment with Heterogeneity-Robust Difference-in-Differences Methods
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank - Economics Department, Bard College - The Levy Economics Institute and Drexel University - Department of Economics & International Business

detail.title: The European Single Market and Intra-EU Trade: An Assessment with Heterogeneity-Robust Difference-in-Differences Methods
detail.abstract: We use heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences (DiD) methods to evaluate the impact of membership in the European Union (EU) Single Market on international trade. On the policy front, we provide evidence that: (i) On average, the EU has been very effective in promoting trade among its member states; (ii) The trade effects of the EU have been long-lasting, but heterogeneous across EU cohorts; and (iii) While the EU has benefited both ‘old’ and ‘new’ members, the increase in the exports from the ‘old’ members to the ‘new’ joiners has been disproportionately larger. From a methods and practical perspective, the contribution of this paper is to introduce a new, fast, and flexible estimation command that combines leading estimation techniques from the gravity literature with recent methods from the heterogeneity-robust DiD literature.

title: Decentralization And Financing of Primary and Secondary Education in the Republic of Macedonia

detail.title: Decentralization And Financing of Primary and Secondary Education in the Republic of Macedonia
detail.abstract: The main aim of the process of Decentralization of education was to improve conditions, quality educational standards and to enable access to education. However, in order the process of decentralization of education to achieve its objectives, is necessary to be accompanied by sufficient fiscal decentralization, sufficient funding versus authorizations by the Local authorities in the sphere of education, exacerbates the efficiency of providing public services. The main aim of this paper is to analyze the theoretical and empirical analysis of the forms of financing of primary and secondary education in the Republic of Macedonia in the time period from the beginning of the process of decentralization since 2005. The paper includes a review of the financial sufficiency for the realization of this comity, the criteria on the basis of which the funds from the central government to the local government are distributed and the criteria for determining the level of education budget at the local level. A number of problems have been identified in the application of current methods and an alternative approach to estimate the cost for student needs has been proposed. In order to make an informed decision about the required levels of resources, research needs to be done to determine the costs associated with the education of students with different levels of need.

title: Responsible Financial Behavior: Similarities and Differences between Youth in Türkiye and Lithuania
affiliations: Balikesir University

detail.title: Responsible Financial Behavior: Similarities and Differences between Youth in Türkiye and Lithuania

publicationDetails.detailsText: Revista Romaneasca pentru Educatie Multidimensionala, volume 17, issue 3, 2025[10.18662/rrem/17.3/1041]

detail.abstract: This research compares the financial behaviors of university students in Lithuania and Türkiye, focusing on each financial behavior individually. The study also examines how gender and income levels affect responsible financial behaviors. The results indicate that Lithuanian students demonstrate more responsible financial behaviors than their Turkish counterparts. Gender does not appear to significantly impact responsible financial behaviors for students in either country; however, a correlation exists between higher income levels and responsible financial behaviors. While Turkish students show more responsible behaviors in terms of budget planning, Lithuanian students excel in responsible savings behavior. Furthermore, Lithuanian students tend to have a more optimistic outlook on their financial futures, whereas Turkish students have lower expectations compared to Lithuanian students. These findings provide valuable insights for educational authorities seeking to improve students' financial knowledge and promote responsible financial behaviors. The results suggest that tailored financial education programs could be developed based on this research.

title: Tariffs as Fiscal Policy
affiliations: UCLA School of Law and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Tariffs as Fiscal Policy
detail.abstract:
The year 2025 brought a remarkable shift in the role of tariffs in the US economy, as the Trump administration simultaneously escalated the use of broad tariffs and ensured that Congress enacted large income tax cuts. This fiscal switch has important implications for the US tax system. While maintaining tariff rates at summer 2025 levels would generate large government revenues, such broad tariffs have significant downsides: Efficiency losses would approach one-third of revenues raised, the tax system would be less progressive, and there would be serious tax administration concerns. The fiscal shift also has significant macroeconomic implications, although probably not the intended ones. Broad tariffs generate a large negative supply shock, simultaneously raising prices and reducing macroeconomic activity.

title: Private Equity, Consumers, and Competition: Evidence from the Nursing Home Industry
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management, San Diego State University and

detail.title: Private Equity, Consumers, and Competition: Evidence from the Nursing Home Industry
detail.abstract:
This paper studies how product market competition shapes the impact of private equity (PE) acquisitions on consumers. We examine nursing home buyouts and observe that PE-owned facilities exhibit greater competitive sensitivity: competing more aggressively when competitive incentives are strong and exploiting market power more aggressively when competitive incentives are weak. We find that PE-owned facilities are more sensitive to local market competition—even when comparing effects only across facilities purchased as part of the same acquisition—and are more responsive to a pro-competitive policy helping consumers compare facilities. This suggests that the competitive sensitivity of acquirers and the concentration of markets where acquisitions occur are important factors contributing to the effects of a merger, as well as that pro-competitive polices can reshape the effects of PE ownership on consumers.

title: Retrenchment, Segregation, and Public Education: A Five-Year Analysis of State Exclusionary School Discipline Legislation
affiliations: University of California Hastings College of Law and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Retrenchment, Segregation, and Public Education: A Five-Year Analysis of State Exclusionary School Discipline Legislation
detail.abstract: Notwithstanding the decision in Brown v. Board of Education formally ending educational segregation and more than two decades of state reform, the legislative landscape protecting children from the harmful consequences of exclusionary school discipline has dramatically shifted in less than five years. From the passage of state “Teacher’s Bills of Rights” to mandatory expulsions, rescission of prior protections, and new categories of removal, a retrenchment of anti-inclusion legislation—and its corollary, educational carcerality—has occurred. While studies of other forms of legislative retrenchment in K–12 public schools, such as anti-Critical Race Theory, Don’t Say Gay, literacy bans, and anti-transgender measures, have drawn sharp attention to the purpose and functionality to erase, exclude, and punish children, unaccounted for within this literature is the simultaneity of new bills that physically segregate children from their public school classrooms and communities. This Article addresses that gap and introduces the first systematic review of regressive state exclusionary school discipline bills proposed from 2020 to 2025. Results of the study include aggregated and disaggregated analyses of fifty-six bills across twenty-four states and reveal a substantial rise in exclusionary school discipline, producing a net result of heightened risk for punishment and structural violence against children as early as age five.

title: The Impact of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) on Economic Growth in Bangladesh

detail.title: The Impact of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) on Economic Growth in Bangladesh

detail.abstract: This study examines the long-term and short-term effects of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) on Bangladesh's economic growth from 1980 to 2024. While FDI is recognized as a key factor for development, its effectiveness depends on the characteristics of the host country. This research uses a mixed-methods approach, combining time-series and sectoral panel data to explore this complex relationship. We apply Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression for initial parameter estimation and a Panel Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) to assess the short-term dynamics and long-term connections, including causality and co-integration.

title: Flow Control: The Work of Collateral in Chinese Overseas Lending
affiliations: Georgetown University Law Center, Georgetown University Law Center, Kiel Institute for the World Economy, Kiel Institute for the World Economy - IFW, College of William & Mary and Kiel Institute for the World Economy

detail.title: Flow Control: The Work of Collateral in Chinese Overseas Lending
detail.abstract: This symposium contribution draws on newly identified debt and security agreements and other primary sources to analyze two episodes of secured overseas lending by Chinese institutions. Together with its companion quantitative study of 620 collateralized debt transactions between Chinese lenders and public sector borrowers in Emerging Market and Developing Economies (EMDEs), it offers a rare window into some of the relationships and practices that animate debates about geopolitics and finance. We show that collateralization is a regular feature of Chinese lending in EMDEs, and that Chinese lenders are far more likely to use control over liquid assets-revenue streams and bank accounts-than ports or mineral deposits to secure risky public and publicly guaranteed (PPG) debt. Transaction structures that give creditors "flow control," or the ability to block or capture foreign currency cashflows, are commonplace in our dataset, and have roots in both early and late 20 th century sovereign debt practice. We trace the design, provenance, and functions of secured credit in a railway construction project in Kenya and a road construction program in Ghana. In the case studies and in the companion dataset, we find that Chinese lenders adapt and scale market-standard tools, experimenting with legal techniques in an effort to maximize recovery, entrench and enhance their leverage in the debtor-creditor relationship. When such experiments succeed, they can give creditors economically and politically significant control over export revenue streams in vulnerable borrowing countries. They can also set off competition for flow control among lenders, which can turn into an asset grab race when the borrower falls in debt distress. Meanwhile, complex collateralized debt structures can obscure governance problems and misaligned incentives, and undercut borrower agency. Their apparent prevalence, and the fact that they have gone virtually unremarked for decades, exposes the fragility of late-20th century international financial architecture.

publicationDetails.detailsText: No, this paper has not appeared, nor has it been accepted to appear, in any Paper Series, Journal, or Book.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the contributions of five leading entrepreneurs in Kyrgyzstan and their impact on the country's economy and society. By analyzing their business trajectories, investment strategies, and social initiatives, this research highlights the crucial role of private entrepreneurship in economic development, job creation, and integration into global markets. The study combines qualitative analysis of media publications, official reports, and available statistical data to construct a comprehensive view of entrepreneurship in Kyrgyzstan. The findings reveal that despite challenges such as corruption, unstable legal frameworks, and limited access to capital, these entrepreneurs have played a transformative role in shaping the socioeconomic environment of the nation.

title: Economic integration in the XXI century

detail.title: Economic integration in the XXI century
detail.abstract:
The study carried out a historical analysis of international cooperation, which revealed a constant need for the economic expansion to new regions. It was proved that since the end of the 19th century, there has been a tendency to abandon violent expansion in favor of international cooperation, which is beneficial not so much due to military-political factors as due to building an effective system of economic penetration into new markets and mutual dependence. The paper examines in detail the differences between integration and close international economic cooperation. It has been established that economic cooperation develops into integration only when regional ties become comparable in importance to national ones. 

An analysis of the practice of international cooperation within the framework of existing integration associations (EU, MERCOSUR, APEC, ASEAN, EAEU, etc.) revealed an increase in attention to the issues of economic security of the integrating countries. This is especially clearly demonstrated by the official documents of the USMCA and the initiatives being implemented within the framework of the SCO. It was found that after the triumph of the ideas of economic integration in the second half of the twentieth century, the ideas of protecting own national interests are more in demand today. In scientific discourse, this concept is commonly referred to as Homeland Economics.

title: Managing Competing Demands: Coping With the Inclusiveness–Efficiency Paradox in Cross-Sector Partnerships
affiliations: Radboud University Nijmegen, Copenhagen Business School and University of Witten/Herdecke

detail.title: Managing Competing Demands: Coping With the Inclusiveness–Efficiency Paradox in Cross-Sector Partnerships
detail.abstract: This article discusses how cross-sector partnerships (CSPs) for sustainability manage the paradoxical tension between stakeholder inclusiveness and administrative efficiency. Drawing on qualitative data from a case study of a CSP focused on urban sustainability, we show how the inclusiveness–efficiency paradox unfolded throughout the studied collaboration. We discuss how the paradox reemerged in a different guise within each phase of the partnership and how three practices of paradox management helped actors to cope with the tension: “customized inviting” (during the formation phase), “sequential including” (during the preparation phase), and “tailored instructing” (during the implementation phase). On the basis of these findings, we argue that (a) the paradox reoccurred throughout the phases of the CSP because the three paradox management practices accentuated boundaries, thereby helping to resolve the paradox temporarily while at the same time creating grounds for the paradox to resurface, and (b) that the three paradox management practices can be theorized as a special type of boundary work that “plays up” relevant differences between actor groups and thereby ensures collaboration.

title: A Contextual Note on the Contribution of Bourdieu’s Theory to Social Development
affiliations: Gandhigram Rural Institute

detail.title: A Contextual Note on the Contribution of Bourdieu’s Theory to Social Development
detail.abstract: The Bourdieu's theory uniquely demonstrates the three pillars, namely Habitus, Capital, and Field, with their interrelationships , and how they impact on social development. In this context, this paper objectively attempts to structure a mind-map in relation to livelihood, social cohesion, and poverty, by citing a possible postwar situation in general. Indicatively, this paper explores the key concepts such as development and its various types, relational aspects of development, civil war, postwar development, livelihoods, social cohesion, poverty, culture, habitus, and the field. This paper effectively highlights the major development-oriented core aspects and variables within a postwar situation, and presents a potential mind-map for future studies, in consideration of Bourdieu's theory as the most suitable framework for exploring their relationships.

title: Macroprudential Policy, Household Credit and House Prices
affiliations: VU University Amsterdam, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, School of Business and Economics and VU University Amsterdam

detail.title: Macroprudential Policy, Household Credit and House Prices
detail.abstract: The paper looks at how changes in credit availability affect house prices. It finds that when lending standards are relaxed, household credit increases, which leads to higher transaction prices, more overbidding (both in number and amount), and faster property sales. As the housing boom progresses, the effect on prices grows because more households take on credit. The impact is especially strong in areas with limited housing supply and low affordability, among buyers who have limited cash but can still access credit, and for more expensive homes. These results support the idea that household demand is driven by credit, and they show that macroprudential policy helps manage systemic risk not only by lowering household debt, but also by slowing house price growth during the economic cycle.

title: Lights Out, Crime Up? Evidence from National Power Outages Data
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: Lights Out, Crime Up? Evidence from National Power Outages Data
detail.abstract: Power outages affect the average US electric customer for eight hours annually. Despite their effects on ambient light and routine activities, no research has identified their effects on public safety. This paper provides the first national-level evidence of power outages' effects on crime using high-resolution outage and crime data from 2018-2023. Exploiting county-day variation in outages and including high-dimensional fixed effects, I find outages increase theft by 0.71%, while reducing assault by 0.72%. This asymmetry reflects mobility shifts in response to outages where residents leave their homes, creating opportunities for property crime while reducing chances of domestic violence.

title: Belief Elicitation as Behavioral Design: Forecasting Others' Actions Reduces Moral Wiggle Room
affiliations: University of California, Merced - Department of Economics

detail.title: Belief Elicitation as Behavioral Design: Forecasting Others' Actions Reduces Moral Wiggle Room
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether eliciting beliefs about others' behavior can reduce the use of moral wiggle room-the justifications that allow individuals to act selfishly while maintaining a positive self-image. Across two incentivized experiments, a moral wiggle room game and a dice-rolling task, belief elicitation reduced information avoidance, dishonesty, and opportunistic behavior. While participants often reported self-serving beliefs after acting selfishly, their appropriateness evaluations remained unchanged, suggesting that belief elicitation does not correct biased expectations but instead preempts their formation by activating latent social norms-contrary to Bayesian models of belief updating. By heightening social image concerns at the moment of choice, belief elicitation constrains moral wiggle room and shifts behavior toward prosocial outcomes. These findings clarify how norms influence ethical decision-making and position belief elicitation as a scalable, low-cost behavioral design tool for curbing opportunism where monitoring is limited.

title: "FOOD FOR PEACE?" CAMBODIA'S 1970S DEBTS TO THE UNITED STATES
affiliations: University of North Carolina School of Law, University of Virginia School of Law and Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies (IHEID) - Department of Economics

detail.title: "FOOD FOR PEACE?" CAMBODIA'S 1970S DEBTS TO THE UNITED STATES

publicationDetails.detailsText: UNC Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of North Carolina Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This is the story of three loans that were made by the United States in the 1970s, under the Food for Peace program, to the embattled Lon Nol regime in Cambodia. Cambodia has since argued the loans were tainted by the United States' bombardment of Cambodian territory and support for Lon Nol's illegitimate regime. It has refused to pay, invoking the international law doctrine of odious debt, asserting the right to disavow this "dirty" debt. The United States, by contrast, maintains that no such legal doctrine exists and that Cambodia must first acknowledge the obligation and begin repayment before any modification can be discussed. Despite this insistence, the United States has never attempted to enforce its claims. The result has been a stalemate, which for many years neither side seemed eager to resolve. In mid 2025 though, a confluence of events has raised the possibility of a shift in the impasse. This case offers an opportunity to test the boundaries of legal doctrines like odious debt and war debt. Mostly, we just think this is a fascinating story.

title: Innovations and Enterprises Performance in Transition Countries, with Special Emphasis on Kosovo: CDM Model Approach
affiliations: University of Kadri Zeka, AAB College and

detail.title: Innovations and Enterprises Performance in Transition Countries, with Special Emphasis on Kosovo: CDM Model Approach
detail.abstract: The main aim of this study is to analyze the impact of innovation and enterprise performance in the transition countries with special emphasis in the case of Kosovo. The innovations play a crucial impact on firm development, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises in countries in transition. This study uses primary data with a specific sample thus the enterprises that operate in Kosovo in order to analyze the relationship between innovations and firm performance. This study was conducted within a six-month period, specifically January 2022-June 2022. The research sample consists of 400 Kosovar enterprises. These enterprises are from different economic sectors, such as production, services, and in terms of size, 80% of them are SMEs. The study used the CDM (Crépon, Duguet and Mairesse) model which includes the fourth phase. The first phase of this model is about the tendencies of enterprises to carry out innovative activities, the second phase is about the enterprises that invested in research and development, the third stage of the model, the conversion of inputs into outputs is analyzed. In the end, the impact of innovation outputs on the performance of the analyzed enterprises is investigated. The study concludes that enterprises that export to the EU and the Western Balkans region are significant, so this positively affects the tendencies of these enterprises for innovative activities, whereas enterprises that are oriented only to the local market, do not present significance and even have a negative relationship with the enterprises' tendencies for innovations. A large part of the enterprises think that innovations have high costs and are even unaffordable therefore this represents a big obstacle for the development of innovations. The lack of qualified personnel and the lack of knowledge about markets and technology represent a big obstacle to the development of innovations, and it even negatively affects the decisions of these enterprises about innovations.

title: How do Developing Country Governments Finance Healthcare while Respecting Fiscal Constraints?

detail.title: How do Developing Country Governments Finance Healthcare while Respecting Fiscal Constraints?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is based on secondary data and publicly available sources only.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Developing countries often face a big challenge: how to expand access to good quality healthcare while also working with very limited budgets. The purpose of this paper is to look at how governments can finance healthcare without creating fiscal problems. To do this, I use a comparative analysis of four countries: Rwanda, Ghana, Thailand, and Mexico. The study is based on the idea of "fiscal space for health" and the three main functions of health financing: revenue collection, pooling of risks, and purchasing of services. In this work, I review traditional methods such as taxation, social health insurance, and out-of-pocket payments, and I also look at more innovative solutions like "sin" taxes, public-private partnerships, external aid, debt swaps, and digital financial inclusion. The results suggest that no single method is enough by itself. Instead, success depends on combining several strategies, such as expanding the tax base while protecting the poor, improving pooling to avoid catastrophic payments, and strengthening governance to make health spending more efficient. The paper concludes by showing that financing healthcare in developing countries is not only an economic problem but also a political one, and that sustainable solutions must be adapted to each country's context.

title: Transforming Traditional Business into Online: The Impact of Covid-19 Pandemic on Consumer Behavior
affiliations: AAB College, University of Prizren "Ukshin HOTI",  and Aleksandër Moisiu University of Durrës

detail.title: Transforming Traditional Business into Online: The Impact of Covid-19 Pandemic on Consumer Behavior
detail.abstract: COVID-19 pandemic well-known worldwide for its serious health consequences is having a profound effect on every sphere of life. Taking into consideration that COVID-19 is harming the labor market and economic activity in general, we also consider that this situation is affecting the personal consumption expenditures in case of Kosovo (Ziberi, Rexha, & Gashi, 2021). The main aim of this paper is to analyze how the customers’ behavior will shift the traditional business to an online one in case of Western Balkan countries with special emphasis on Kosovo, North Macedonia and Albania. The study considered the mixed methods using the questionnaire as a method for primary data collection in a random sample of citizens from countries in the analysis. The questionnaire was distributed online using social media in a sample of 1250 respondents. The paper uses the SPSS software for data analysis and hypotheses testing. The study comes to the conclusion that buying behavior is changing due to the imposed measures by governance due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Thus, the confidence in online shopping has increased significantly which is a good base for further recommendations for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to start reworking selling strategies and to shift their activity from purely traditional to hybrid one — traditional and online — promoting so better the traditional business. Our findings also are in line with a study by Bytyçi (2020) who stated that the consumers in case of the Republic of Kosovo prefer online shopping for one main reason — time loss reduction.

title: A Temporary VAT Cut as Unconventional Fiscal Policy
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, University Bonn, Deutsche Bundesbank, Deutsche Bundesbank, University Tuebingen and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: A Temporary VAT Cut as Unconventional Fiscal Policy
detail.abstract: We exploit Germany's temporary three-percentage-point VAT cut in the second half of 2020 to study the spending response to unconventional fiscal policy. We use survey and scanner data on household consumption expenditures and their perceived pass-through of the tax change into prices, and a RANK model to quantify the effects of this VAT policy. The survey and scanner data show that the temporary VAT reduction led to a relative increase in durable and, to a lesser extent, semidurable spending for individuals with high perceived pass-through. According to the RANK model, the VAT policy increased total aggregate consumption spending by 4.4 percent on impact.

title: Indexical Collapse: Reference Disappears, Authority Remains in Predictive Systems
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: Indexical Collapse: Reference Disappears, Authority Remains in Predictive Systems
detail.abstract: This article introduces the concept of Indexical Collapse, the disappearance of reference in predictive systems. Indexical such as pronouns, demonstratives, and tenses presuppose a contextual anchor, yet predictive language models reproduce them without connection to reality. The outcome is a collapse of reference that paradoxically produces authority effects in law, medicine, and governance. By analyzing judicial transcripts, medical reports, institutional records, and chatbot interactions generated by AI, the paper proposes a framework for pragmatic auditing of predictive outputs. It establishes thresholds for acceptable referential absence in critical domains, positioning Indexical Collapse as a central category for evaluating the legitimacy of predictive discourse.

title: Untangling Privacy and Competition
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - School of Law and

detail.title: Untangling Privacy and Competition
detail.abstract:
This Article argues that competition law, contrary to the hopes of policymakers and scholars that it offers a powerful tool to combat privacy harms, operates as an anti-privacy framework. Far from a means to address widespread surveillance by market-dominant platforms and other data-intensive firms that monetize the collection and analysis of personal information, competition law’s analysis systematically privileges corporate interests at the expense of consumer protection.

This analysis proceeds in two parts. First, the Article identifies the specific competition law concerns raised in recent regulatory enforcement actions and private litigation involving Big Tech, as well as leading scholarship, regarding the ways in which large technology firms secure, enhance, and exploit market power through collection and use of personal data. It then provides an analytic framework that identifies circumstances in which competition concerns align with privacy concerns, pointing in the same regulatory and logical direction, and other circumstances in which those two sets of concerns misalign: where remedies for one might harm the other. Our framework untangles these two sets of concerns and reveals that a majority of competition arguments misalign with privacy. In some misalignment scenarios competition concerns are merely orthogonal to those of privacy, but there is every reason to expect that privacy will be harmed rather than promoted. In others, competition and privacy directly conflict, meaning that promoting competition directly degrades privacy.

Second, the Article reveals two fundamental analytic errors that regulators, courts, and commentators make about privacy in a market setting. These errors dictate privacy-destroying outcomes, even in the instances in which privacy and competition concerns do align.

In the first error, regulators adopt a cramped understanding of the right to privacy as either a superficial concept limited to issues like consent, consumer choice, or data security, or as a means to broader economic goals rather than an essential value on its own terms. Thus, they fail to comprehend privacy as freedom from surveillance. In the second error, competition regulators prioritize markets for surveillance over markets for privacy, either through an agnosticism regarding the substance of the market and a resulting choice to promote the more lucrative and thriving market for surveillance; or through a conceptual confusion between surveillance and privacy markets that obscures the surveillance market’s privacy harms.

These errors combine, we show, in a harsh outcome: that privacy concerns are credited in competition analysis only when doing so promotes the health and competitiveness of privacy-eviscerating surveillance markets. The resulting regulatory imbalance ultimately reinforces the dominance of surveillance-driven business models at the expense of consumer and civil rights.

This analysis underscores the conclusion that privacy cannot be effectively regulated through the back door of competition. Rather, the market for personal data should be regulated directly, as we do in other contexts plagued by market failures and harmful underlying behaviors.

title: Shortage, Liquidity, and the Effectiveness of Monetary Policy: Evidence from the U.S. Commodity Futures Markets
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt - Faculty of Economics and Business Administration and

detail.title: Shortage, Liquidity, and the Effectiveness of Monetary Policy: Evidence from the U.S. Commodity Futures Markets
detail.abstract: This paper is the first to document that monetary policy shocks do not significantly affect commodity futures markets when they are in backwardation, that is, when futures prices fall below spot prices. Since backwardation is a market-based signal of supply constraints, reflecting a premium for immediate delivery due to tight supply or low inventories, this finding suggests a new channel for understanding the effects of monetary policy under supply shortages. We emphasize the role of the basis by extending the inventory-arbitrage channel of monetary policy proposed by Frankel (2008). Under backwardation, producers maintain minimal buffer stocks and little incentive to accumulate inventories, given that front-month futures trade above deferred contracts. By contrast, under contango, monetary tightening may lead producers to secure selling prices in advance and release inventories before the anticipated spot price decline is priced into futures. Consistent with this, we find that monetary policy shocks are significant only under contango. This main result also holds when we extend our analysis to aggregated macroeconomic price indicators such as the Personal Consumption Expenditures Index and the Producer Price Index. To further demonstrate the link between the basis and supply constraints, we construct an Inventory Constraint Index, defined as the cross-sectional mean of the basis. Our food-specific index closely tracks the U.S. Stocks-to-Use Ratio from the World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates. We also evaluate an alternative mechanism, namely the turnover-liquidity channel documented by Lagos and Zhang (2020), as well as the illiquidity premium. Our findings are consistent with the existence of an illiquidity premium, as more illiquid commodities are more susceptible to monetary policy shocks. Yet even after controlling for liquidity, the distinction between contango and backwardation continues to play a significant role.

title: The Rule of Thumb: Private Consumption as A Driving Force of the Economic Growth of Western Balkan Countries
affiliations: AAB College,  and AAB College

detail.title: The Rule of Thumb: Private Consumption as A Driving Force of the Economic Growth of Western Balkan Countries
detail.abstract: Private consumption is considered one of the main drivers of economic growth in Western Balkan countries. The main aim of this study is to estimate the impact of private consumption on the economic growth of the Western Balkans, including the North Macedonia, Kosovo, Albania, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Serbia. Housing wealth was even the main driver of total private consumption in the European Union (EU) countries as a whole (Barradas, 2017). Based on an extensive literature review for panel data, this study uses econometric models with fixed effect, random effect, and Hausman-Taylor test. The data are taken from the World Development Indicators by country (The World Bank, n.d.) and cover the period 2010–2019. Based on the Hausman-Taylor test, the model that fits a small sample as in our case is chosen as the fixed effect. The results of the estimator show that a 1% increase in final consumption leads to a 0.43% increase in gross domestic product (GDP) growth and that, on the other hand, a 1% increase in the employment rate increases GDP by 0.11%. The most important domestic factor continues to be private consumption, driven by record levels in the labour market and further strengthening of household purchasing power (Bank of Slovenia, 2020). The study concludes that private consumption is the main driver of economic growth and sustainability in the case of the Western Balkans.

reference: Columbia Business School Research Paper No. 5551159
title: The Illusion of Foresight: Macroeconomic Indicators, Predictive Power, and Misinterpretation Pitfalls
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: The Illusion of Foresight: Macroeconomic Indicators, Predictive Power, and Misinterpretation Pitfalls

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Business School Research Paper No. 5551159
publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the predictive power of macroeconomic indicators in forecasting financial market performance, emphasizing the distinction between economic and market forecasting. Drawing on insights from financial practitioners and academic literature, we analyze which indicators hold predictive value and highlight common fallacies that investors and analysts encounter, particularly those related to low sample sizes and reliance on unreliable or misinterpreted data. Key findings suggest that while certain indicators, such as yield curve inversions, exhibit some predictive reliability, their utility is limited by broad time horizons and market-specific dynamics. The paper also critiques the pervasive tendency to overfit narratives to macroeconomic data, leading to flawed conclusions. We advocate for a disciplined approach that prioritizes market fundamentals, such as earnings per share reactions and return on invested capital over sensationalized or poorly substantiated data. By addressing these issues, we aim to provide a framework for investors to navigate the noise of macroeconomic forecasting and focus on actionable, evidence-based insights.

reference: Virginia Public Law and Legal Theory Research Paper Forthcoming
title: State Aid Enforcement After Apple
affiliations: University of Virginia School of Law

detail.title: State Aid Enforcement After Apple

declarations.declarationOfInterest: non
declarations.funderStatement: UVA, NYU

publicationDetails.detailsText: Virginia Public Law and Legal Theory Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Virginia Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This is the text of Ruth Mason's Tillinghast Lecture, delivered at NYU School of Law in October 2025.  The lecture frames the EU's anti-subsidy rules (state-aid) as involving balancing act when subsidies are delivered as tax savings: the EU protects free movement and a level playing field, yet Member States retain primary tax-design powers (rates, bases, allocation methods). 

Procedurally, the Commission must prove a selective advantage and often does so by constructing a “reference system” and identifying a derogation—an approach that mirrors tax-expenditure analysis.  But recent cases have pushed this method into controversial territory because those cases concerned what tax-expenditure analysis labels "structural rules." Structural rules are the deep architecture of the tax system—such as tax rates, taxable units, and methods of allocating income—for which there are no ready reference bases.  The Commission's search for new methods that can handle structural tax rules has led to ambiguity, accusations of political motives, baseline fights, and recoveries that rely on  debatable premises.  Mason's solution—described in more detail in a forthcoming book—enlists alternative methodologies that can separate true distortions (tariff equivalents or subsidies for interstate over in-state commerce) from mere mismatches or policy differences between states. Getting the method right is not a mere academic problem: it enhances predictability for business, preserves the Commission’s legitimacy, and better serves the single market’s neutrality goals.

title: Climate Accounting and Domestic Incentives for Agricultural GHG Mitigation
affiliations: Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU) - Department of Economics and University of Saskatchewan

detail.title: Climate Accounting and Domestic Incentives for Agricultural GHG Mitigation
detail.abstract: The current global greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting framework excludes CO₂ removed and stored in harvested crops, as well as CO₂ released when crops are consumed. This omission creates flawed incentives, encouraging deforestation and higher global emissions. Net Ecosystem Emission (NEE) accounting, which explicitly includes these biogenic fluxes, could address this gap. We develop a three-region partial equilibrium model of the world vegetable oil market to examine how GHG accounting regimes and green procurement strategies influence agricultural GHG mitigation policy and global emission outcomes. Holding the policies in the other regions constant, we simulate and compare optimal (welfare maximizing) EU policies where GHG emissions are measured using UNFCCC accounting versus NEE accounting. We then use the model to simulate the effectiveness of prohibiting the imports of high GHG emission vegetable oils on domestic and global GHG emissions. Our simulations show that EU policies designed to optimally mitigate UNFCCC-measured GHG emissions will consistently result in higher world vegetable oil prices and increased global agricultural GHG emissions. In contrast, EU policies designed to optimally mitigate NEE-measured GHG emissions will result in lower world vegetable oil prices and reduced global GHG emissions. Import bans on high-emission oils, however, have little effect on global emissions due to trade diversion. These results highlight the need to reform UNFCCC accounting to enable more effective agricultural GHG mitigation.

title: The Post-Scarcity Catalyst: Permanently Solving Economic Scarcity through Fusion Energy Adoption
affiliations: The Open University - Faculty of Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics

detail.title: The Post-Scarcity Catalyst: Permanently Solving Economic Scarcity through Fusion Energy Adoption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicting interests

keywords: The Post-Scarcity Catalyst: Permanently Solving Economic Scarcity Through Fusion Energy Adoption Author: [Rasheeq B. N. N. Choudhury] Date: September 13

detail.abstract: For centuries, the fundamental axiom of economics has been the problem of scarcityunlimited human wants versus limited resources. This preprint posits that the successful development and global adoption of commercial nuclear fusion energy represent a paradigm-shifting technological breakthrough capable of permanently solving the problem of economic scarcity. We argue that fusion energy, characterized by its near-limitless fuel supply, immense energy density, inherent safety, and minimal environmental impact, can decouple human civilization from its dependence on finite energy resources. This decoupling would cascade through all sectors of the economy, drastically reducing the cost base for essential goods like food, water, materials, and transportation. By analysing the downstream effects on production, recycling, and environmental management, we demonstrate that the primary constraints of scarcity can be alleviated. We conclude that the remaining challenges are not technical or economic, but rather political, social, and ideological in transitioning to a new economic model predicated on abundance rather than scarcity.

title: Spatial Spillovers and Determinants of Sovereign ESG Performance: Evidence from a Spatial Durbin Model
affiliations: University of Pécs - Faculty of Business and Economics and University of Pécs

detail.title: Spatial Spillovers and Determinants of Sovereign ESG Performance: Evidence from a Spatial Durbin Model
detail.abstract: Understanding the determinants of Sovereign Environmental, Social, and Governance (SESG) performance is crucial for advancing global sustainability. Despite the increasing interest, most studies concentrate on firms, neglecting the spatial interdependencies among countries. This study addresses this gap by investigating how national attributes and regional interactions collectively influence SESG performances. We analyze a panel of 107 countries from 2000 to 2022 using a spatial econometric framework. The use of Global and local Moran’s I and Getis–Ord Gi* statistics reveals a notable geographic clustering of SESG performance. This observation justifies the adoption of a Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) with two-way fixed effects. Model selection tests identified the SDM as the most appropriate specification, indicating that a country’s SESG performance is affected not only by its own characteristics but also by those of neighboring nations. Our results validate a U-shaped relationship between economic growth and SESG, consistent with the Environmental Kuznets Curve. Notably, we uncover significant spatial spillovers, indicating that economic growth in neighboring countries has a negative effect (“race-to-the-bottom”). At the same time, their investments in climate adaptation and renewable energy generate positive spillovers. Political integration fosters cooperation, whereas economic globalization may exacerbate negative externalities. These findings underscore the inherent regional interdependence of SESG performance. Thus, effective sustainability policies necessitate coordinated regional strategies, including harmonized standards, technology-sharing platforms, and regional cooperation initiatives. Neglecting spatial interdependencies can lead to ineffective policy interventions and worsen regional disparities in sustainable development outcomes.

title: Identifying Terms-of-Trade Shocks with Foreign Weather: Implications for Monetary Policy
affiliations: University of Florida - Department of Economics

detail.title: Identifying Terms-of-Trade Shocks with Foreign Weather: Implications for Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: How do the terms of trade (ToT) affect the macroeconomy, and how should monetary policy respond? I identify exogenous ToT shocks for 48 economies by combining a rich set of high-frequency weather shocks from foreign territories with bilateral trade flows. I apply machine learning methods to map high-dimensional weather shocks into low dimensional components that predict future ToT growth out of sample, while avoiding overfitting. Using panel local projections, I show that negative ToT shocks are contractionary and inflationary, creating a policy tradeoff under floating exchange rates. A shock that causes a 10% decline in the ToT one year ahead raises prices by 3% and reduces economic activity by 1.5% in the medium run (5 years). Stabilizing inflation requires preemptive contractionary policy of 46 bps, offsetting 90% of the shock’s cumulative effects, while closing the output gap calls for preemptive expansionary policy of 20 bps, neutralizing 70% respectively.

title: Erdogan’s Fight with Global Media During Elections: Lessons for the World
affiliations: Department of International Relations, University of Dhaka

detail.title: Erdogan’s Fight with Global Media During Elections: Lessons for the World
